chapters.question_prompt: How do tax-sale overages arise, and how does a recovery agent help an owner claim the money?
chapters.title: How the Surplus Recovery Business Works
chapters.subtitle: Tax-sale excess proceeds, owner recovery, the agent's role, and introductory find-contact-claim workflows.
chapters.executive_summary: Ted Thomas, Bob Diamond, Tax Sale Academy, and Overage Acquisition describe the same starting point: an auction generates more money than the debt being collected, leaving excess proceeds that an eligible claimant can pursue. The recovery business connects records, owners, agreements, and claims rather than buying the property. Eric Richardson emphasizes accessible county records and repeatable outreach; Spencer Vann separates data, sales, and processing. Practitioner economics range from free records and inexpensive skip tracing to paid mail campaigns and attorney-led buyouts. Their disagreements matter: Diamond withholds the money's source before contracting, while SurplusFundsRiches favors disclosure and upfront good-faith payments. State selection, creditor priority, mistaken identities, stale lists, and county processing delays determine whether a promising balance becomes a collected fee.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The business begins with excess cash after an auction, not with the recovery agent buying a house. Tax Sale Academy defines excess proceeds as money paid above what the county is owed, including back taxes, interest, fees, and expenses. Its example uses a $1,000 obligation and a $2,500 sale, leaving $1,500. Overage Acquisition uses a larger illustration: Tom owes $10,000 in property taxes, the property sells for $100,000, and the difference is a $90,000 overage. Both explanations separate the auction buyer's acquisition from the former owner's possible recovery. The buyer receives the property; the recovery operator works on the remaining money and the person entitled to claim it. Ted Thomas makes the same distinction with a property worth $100,000, bidding beginning at $10,000, and a sale at $20,000. The buyer may be pleased with the purchase, but Thomas directs attention to the $10,000 above the tax amount. These are the speakers' teaching examples, not reported completed claims. Their shared starting point is an actual sale producing excess proceeds, followed by a separate recovery process. The agent's work concerns that second process rather than bidding, financing a purchase, or reselling the auctioned property. [snu6i8Dp6h8 @ 00:00:18] [zed9ZTbgUfI @ 00:00:50] [d5TLZqkPX14 @ 00:08:22]

The next shared premise is an information and contact problem: money can exist without the former owner knowing how to retrieve it. Overagesorg describes inadequate notice and owners leaving funds behind; its finder model is to locate those owners and assist with collection for a service fee. Unclaimed CEO explains the practical break in notification: county mail often goes to the last known address, which is the very home the person has lost. The speaker says county offices lack the bandwidth to hunt people down, creating a role for investigators who can find them. Eric Richardson gives a concrete version from a client they helped: a Miami-Dade notice identified $21,215 from a February 18, 2021 tax-deed sale and said the office would hold it for 120 days. Richardson then explains that letters can be addressed to the foreclosed property. This is why the business is more than downloading a balance: the operator must connect the record to a reachable person. Across these accounts, finding the money and reaching its possible claimant are separate jobs. Richardson's example also shows an actual county notice, rather than treating every county as silent or every owner as already informed. [FOHcsz8xKFk @ 00:00:00] [ug2uUK_s2yk @ 00:02:13] [vs2o6Zz48Oc @ 00:05:16]

The operating sequence is equally consistent: obtain records, identify and locate the claimant, establish a working relationship, secure documents, and pursue the claim. Bob Diamond describes public-record lists carrying an amount, a property address or tax identification number, usually a person's name, and the sale date. Their workflow moves from those records to skip tracing, outreach, a signed contract package, submission, and follow-up. Spencer Vann organizes essentially the same workload into data, sales, and processing. Data includes filtering, a CRM, and skip tracing; sales means getting people to work with the business; processing means turning agreement into signed documents and money. Vann specifically flags the gap between someone saying yes and actually signing. Richardson adds a useful starting condition: choose a county where results are accessible, the claim form has instructions, and existing claims can be checked. Their emphasis is not merely finding an impressive list but understanding how that county publishes results and accepts claims. These accounts put the beginner's foundation in a working records-to-payment process. Diamond's list provides the starting information, Richardson's county screen makes the process navigable, and Vann's three-part framework keeps research, client acquisition, and claim completion from being mistaken for the same task. [eLVlXKRQOTI @ 00:07:01] [GG8f_umaBfY @ 00:02:42] [_vsvjD8JvgU @ 00:02:11]

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Start the research with the language the county uses. Diamond's search pattern is county, state, and 'excess funds list'; their examples include DeKalb County Georgia, Hamilton County Ohio, and Broward County Florida. The resulting list gives names and amounts before the operator looks up contact information. SurplusFundsRiches broadens the search vocabulary to overbids, surplus funds, mortgage overages, tax-sale overages, tax-deed overages, excess funds, and excess proceeds. When an online list is unavailable, the channel contacts whoever held the sale and asks by phone or email. Its 'one and done' method uses a list obtained from one county as a sample to show another county what is being requested. Overage Acquisition supplies the parcel-based route: find the county's excess-proceeds list, use parcel numbers to identify previous owners, and then locate those people. Its paid alternative is Excess Elite, described as delivering daily nationwide leads, skip-traced contacts, phone-number checks against the do-not-call registry, and AI analysis of deals, debts, and liens. The channel presents paid data and manual county research as budget-dependent alternatives. SurplusFundsRiches also recommends requesting lists directly because the extra request can reach records other operators are unwilling to pursue. [1Pp-cjYnY2k @ 00:04:52] [4W8c0I28pxQ @ 00:11:07] [q2gk3WmK5xs @ 00:03:26]

For contact research, Richardson gives a concrete low-budget stack rather than requiring a large initial data purchase. True People Search is their free option; they also name BeenVerified, Intelius, and batch skip tracing. Their Skip Matrix example, using the code Surplus, costs about $14 to $15 for 100 leads instead of spending four, five, or possibly ten hours researching manually. SurplusFundsRiches takes a more specialized approach: IDI Data is its first stop for claimant phone numbers and addresses, Microbilt is favored for possible relatives or associates, and Whitepages Premium is praised for reverse-address searches after recent sales. The same channel says TLO has tightened access and generally requires a private investigator or attorney. For outreach economics, a student in Richardson's webinar itemizes a mailed letter at 85 cents: 20 cents for a virtual assistant's skip tracing, 58 cents postage, five cents for the envelope, and one cent each for paper and ink. The student budgets $850 for 1,000 letters and aims for a $10,000 deal. That is the student's campaign plan, while Richardson separately points out that calls can be made without buying postage. The accounts describe different research and contact choices, with their own quoted costs. [_vsvjD8JvgU @ 00:02:40] [4W8c0I28pxQ @ 00:33:27] [vs2o6Zz48Oc @ 00:18:26]

The contact-to-claim handoff begins with a clear compensation proposal. Diamond's sample invitation says the company found money with the person's name on it, works for a percentage, requires no deposit, and gets paid only if successful. The speaker then moves to hiring the business and applying for the money. Overage Acquisition teaches calling first, maintaining contact by text or email, showing auction results or county or court records as evidence, and sending an agreement that states terms and fees. Its county follow-up routine is specific: keep documents organized, obtain a staff contact where possible, use priority mail with tracking and delivery proof, and send additional requested documents immediately. Diamond distinguishes the filing routes. An administrative claim goes to the department that conducted the tax foreclosure, often through a short claim form; a judicial claim involves money held in court and an attorney doing the claim. Diamond favors administrative claims for beginners because judicial claims bring attorney costs. The paperwork they name includes a fee agreement, power of attorney, assignment, and letter of direction. In their model, the recovery reaches the business before the client's portion is sent out. These are Diamond's mechanics, alongside Overage Acquisition's documented outreach and county-follow-up routine. sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest disagreement is whether to reveal where the money sits before the claimant signs. Overagesorg explicitly teaches keeping the information secret and securing a contract before divulging it. Diamond reports having tested the opposite approach: after the team disclosed the source, prospects stopped answering, and later checks showed claims being made soon after the calls. Diamond therefore leads with a potentially recoverable refund and withholds its source. SurplusFundsRiches takes the opposing position. Its mailing identifies court-held funds, the foreclosure that created them, the property address, and the amount. The channel argues that vague claims of secret money produce distrust. Its answer to being bypassed is not secrecy but a different offer: an upfront structured buyout, good-faith money, and an attorney handling retrieval. Overage Acquisition also teaches disclosure, telling operators to provide sales results, county lists, or court documents rather than merely asserting that money exists. These are genuinely different sales systems. Diamond ties source protection to an observed circumvention problem, while the disclosure operators tie proof to credibility. The distinction reaches beyond wording: SurplusFundsRiches supports its open-book pitch with money paid to the claimant before final recovery, whereas Diamond describes a contingent-fee invitation without a client deposit. [8Xmv6tj4900 @ 00:00:00] [3GWaY7tvULM @ 00:07:31] [4W8c0I28pxQ @ 00:36:50] [q2gk3WmK5xs @ 00:04:46]

Market choice is another split, beginning with what the speakers mean by 'surplus funds.' Richardson distinguishes foreclosure surplus from unclaimed state funds and includes tax, mortgage, and HOA foreclosures in the former category. Vann deliberately uses the broader term to include mortgage funds, tax funds, state-held funds, and bankruptcy funds, then recommends state funds for beginners. Their reasons are available contracts, accessible lead lists, simpler processing, and usually no attorney requirement. Vann also acknowledges lower commission limits, describing state-fund caps of 10 to 20 percent in most states. Diamond instead recommends starting with administrative overage claims and tells beginners to skip Kansas, South Carolina, and California. Richardson says the business can be worked in all 50 states, while insisting operators first understand claim procedures, fee restrictions, and timing. These recommendations are not one shared state-selection rule. Richardson's accessible-county approach asks whether the records and filing instructions are workable; Diamond's approach avoids specific places and favors administrative processing; Vann changes the beginner's initial niche altogether. Vann still permits a tax-fund or mortgage-fund start when that is the operator's chosen focus, but repeatedly returns to picking one market and sticking with it instead of continually changing states and niches. [_vsvjD8JvgU @ 00:00:38] [GG8f_umaBfY @ 00:22:52] [GG8f_umaBfY @ 00:25:05] [qGPsbhsEAVQ @ 00:01:18]

The collection structure changes both the fee conversation and who advances money. Diamond describes fee agreements, powers of attorney, assignments, and directions that route recovered money to the business before paying the client's share. SurplusFundsRiches criticizes that model, saying third-party checks and finder caps can obstruct it. Its alternative pays 10 percent of the gross amount upfront, normally within a week or two after signing, and usually another 40 to 50 percent after successful retrieval. The channel always uses attorneys and says its structured buyouts fall outside finder caps. Those are the channel's claims about its own structure, not a position shared by every speaker. Unclaimed CEO instead illustrates California with a fee of up to 10 percent and payment after the claim succeeds. Outreach preferences divide the operators too. Diamond combines mail, Facebook messages, and phone conversations. SurplusFundsRiches reports little success with texting and no success with social media, preferring postcards and an organized contact rotation. Its rotation hits prospects several times initially, continues every two weeks, and refreshes skip tracing around three months. The practical contrast is between distinct offers and operating routines, not a universal percentage, mandatory communication channel, or single way to receive the recovered funds. sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: A list entry is not the same thing as a payable client file. Diamond identifies the wrong person as the team's most common problem: junior instead of senior, or one John P. Smith instead of another. The team then needs the actual owner's participation rather than the signature already obtained. Diamond also reports mortgage companies or other competing claimants appearing and preventing the anticipated recovery. SurplusFundsRiches makes ownership and debt research central for that reason. It checks who owned the property at the sale, whether recorded debt was satisfied, and whether the listed name still represents the person entitled to pursue the proceeds. The channel's numerical example is a $50,000 overage with a $20,000 unpaid HELOC: it describes setting aside the debt and pursuing $30,000 rather than treating the entire balance as the owner's money. Tax Sale Academy independently notes that some states allow former lienholders priority over the former owner. Together these accounts identify two distinct checks: the person must be the right claimant, and the balance may face other claims. Diamond's firsthand identity errors and creditor appearances explain why a reachable name and a signed agreement do not always produce the expected payment. [eLVlXKRQOTI @ 00:04:25] [4W8c0I28pxQ @ 00:27:29] [snu6i8Dp6h8 @ 00:01:10]

The contact bottleneck is not theoretical. Thomas describes the difficulty of reaching former owners, earning trust, and asking for a fee from someone who does not yet know or like the finder. They also report county employees who resist information requests, making rapport and persistence part of the work. Vann's student example shows how much effort one difficult contact can consume. Belinda tried numerous skip-tracing services, repeatedly received wrong numbers, and finally found a working number through a batch service. The person then denied being the right individual because they thought the call was a scam. Vann says the conversation continued for about an hour before agreement and documents, describing a prospective $50,000 commission rather than an already received payout. SurplusFundsRiches reports a different bottleneck in its own outreach: texting had produced little success and social media none. The channel responds with mail, calls, repeated contact, and refreshed tracing rather than assuming every communication method performs equally. These accounts place the difficulty in locating and persuading actual people, not merely possessing a list. They also keep the work visible: wrong numbers, skepticism, unanswered approaches, and difficult records requests all occur before a claim can be completed. [p9uUtcmNpbk @ 00:03:28] [p9uUtcmNpbk @ 00:05:55] [GG8f_umaBfY @ 00:16:21] [4W8c0I28pxQ @ 00:38:49]

Timing and economics need the same attention as the headline balance. Richardson's Miami-Dade example began with a $21,215 notice but ended with a $20,339 check after the amount changed. SurplusFundsRiches warns that old lists can contain funds already claimed and that mortgage opening bids can be below the actual debt, defeating simple opening-bid subtraction. It also reports lengthy retrieval delays in difficult locations and builds a title recheck into its buyout process before advancing good-faith money. Diamond's own claim-size descriptions differ: one account gives an average a little above $100,000, while the 2024 discussion gives a mathematical average of $52,000 and approximately $20,000 in revenue upon success. Those figures describe different reported business results, not one interchangeable benchmark. Diamond's low-cost contingent model and SurplusFundsRiches' cash-advance model also carry different outlays. The latter says it would rather spend $150 checking title and discover additional debt than advance thousands and find the money cannot be collected. The shared operational point is concrete: a posted amount can change, an old balance may already be gone, and money advanced before retrieval is a real exposure in the buyout approach. Each operator's fee story belongs with that operator's costs and collection process. [vs2o6Zz48Oc @ 00:06:11] [4W8c0I28pxQ @ 00:17:41] [1Pp-cjYnY2k @ 00:03:07] [3GWaY7tvULM @ 00:12:22]

chapters.question_prompt: How can a beginner start a tax overage or surplus funds recovery business with little or no money, understand realistic earnings and overlooked challenges, handle claims when an owner has died, and learn from partnerships, mentorship programs, and reported first-deal and first-year results?
chapters.title: Starting and Growing a Surplus Funds Recovery Business
chapters.subtitle: Beginner guides to tax overages and surplus funds recovery, starting with little or no money, realistic earning potential, reported deal results, deceased-owner claims, partnerships, and mentorship.
chapters.executive_summary: Alfred Taren, Eric Richardson, and Nakia describe the same operating chain: find surplus, locate the entitled person, earn their trust, and move the claim. Richardson teaches free county lists and free skip tracing, with contingency fees commonly described as 15%–30%. Sean reports roughly $300,000 recovered and $80,000 in fees across 12 deals; Matthew reports eight contracts and approximately $60,000 expected, not collected. Their playbooks diverge on preparation, marketing, staffing, and payment control. BizMove builds around AI and a website; Taren puts calls ahead of branding. Deceased-owner work ranges from deed-and-death-date analysis to attorney-led probate. Anthony's missing-ID problem, Fullmer's late-arriving first-year income, and Shawn Bougie's 46-email probate case show why signed agreements, recovery totals, and spendable earnings are different milestones.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The common business is a locating-and-filing service, not a property purchase. Alfred Taren divides each deal into research, conversation, and filing: identify the sale, confirm the surplus, find the person, earn enough trust to help, and move the paperwork. They call the conversation the business because research and filing can be systematized or handed off. Taren also separates foreclosure and tax-sale surplus from forgotten bank accounts and utility deposits held as state unclaimed property [8-8koApqnYA @ 00:01:59]. BizMove describes tax overages as sale proceeds above taxes and fees, with the recovery service locating, notifying, and assisting former owners for a fee [01plOr9pFjQ @ 00:00:22]. Surplus Funds Academy adds the distribution side: identify cases through foreclosure records and court documents, pursue the claim process, then distribute funds to the entitled parties, which can include former owners, lienholders, or other creditors [8Rn25K08ct4 @ 00:01:26]. Nakia's working sequence is equally direct: find the money, inform the former owner, assemble what the claim requires, and retain the contingency fee for that service. Their own research uses a paid platform, but their explanation places the service in the research, contact, and assistance rather than in owning the underlying property [c50hZiiw2FU @ 00:03:57].

A beginner does not have to buy a national lead package before making contact. Eric Richardson's zero-dollar route starts with county websites, searching surplus funds, excess funds, and excess proceeds lists, then calling or emailing counties when necessary. They acknowledge that not every county supplies a free list and that free skip tracing is not always the most efficient route. TruePeopleSearch supplies possible phone numbers, emails, and addresses; the next task is to explain the service accurately by phone [sK5PqCLSzzg @ 00:00:40]. Taren starts with a few counties, the actual county claim forms, and enough confirmed properties to understand the process. Their starter list is only 20–30 names, followed by an opening that sounds natural rather than robotic [8-8koApqnYA @ 00:08:00]. Richardson's separate no-money walkthrough specifies matching the former owner's name and city before searching, including checking whether a county lists last names first. It then moves through outreach, an agreed percentage, notarized documents, and mailing [1fbTnvEjC7M @ 00:02:24]. Both routes put public records and actual contact ahead of an elaborate operation. Richardson permits pen-and-paper tracking while recommending a CRM; Taren postpones the LLC until there are live prospects and money on the way rather than making entity formation the first productive milestone.

Repeated contact and a working claim pipeline recur more consistently than any single software choice. Matthew tells Nick Fullmer that their minimum target is one contract sent each week, with additional contracts pursued even after that target is reached. Their working sequence is phone call, text, letter, then another pass, organized through sections in Evernote. They describe concentrated work blocks rather than treating occasional outreach as a complete business [vd__NHmQYgM @ 00:13:03]. Christopher likewise puts the conversation at the center, reporting a target of at least 100 calls daily while admitting that trustee and attorney work sometimes interrupts it. One claim above $200,000 came through a relative and a returned voicemail; discarding those indirect contacts would have discarded the connection [uhyVFTeepew @ 00:02:57]. Nakia identifies a different version of the same stoppage: people spend hours, days, and months consuming information without starting. Their remedy is a plan, accountability, and a clear next step [c50hZiiw2FU @ 00:00:42]. Richardson adds that waiting for the first payment before pursuing another claim stops the pipeline from developing. Court schedules can leave the first month, or even the next, at zero despite work having been completed. Their instruction is to keep stacking claims every week while earlier files move through the system [lFoZDRAGylo @ 00:01:49].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Start the research at the county and carry it through to entitlement, not just a promising sale price. Richardson searches surplus funds list, overbid list, overage list, and excess proceeds list; their ChatGPT instruction asks for links to counties with lists rather than merely county names. They also track auctions and request sale results or funds held in the court registry [R8B06ovsDXI @ 00:20:59]. BizMove proposes Octoparse or ParseHub for collecting owner information, sale dates, and surplus amounts, and gives a ChatGPT prompt for a Python script extracting names and amounts from a tax-sale PDF [01plOr9pFjQ @ 00:02:35]. Richardson's validation sequence then checks that the sale actually closed to a third-party bidder, checks judicial dockets for an existing claim, and searches for liens, second mortgages, or home equity lines. They distinguish Propwire's mortgage information from fuller lien reports and describe county-recorder searches under individual or entity names, not addresses [R8B06ovsDXI @ 00:26:24]. Taren pairs this work with reading the county's own filing instructions, especially notarization and original-document requirements [8-8koApqnYA @ 00:08:00]. Richardson also warns against treating every opening bid as the actual debt: the surplus calculation depends on confirming what was owed, and nonjudicial cases require contact with the trustee rather than assuming the county holds the necessary records.

The outreach mechanics are specific enough to run without inventing a polished sales performance. Richardson's webinar favors bullet points: introduce yourself and the company, verify the former owner, ask whether they know about the auction and surplus, explain what happened, describe contingency payment, and send proof. Their packet includes company details, supporting evidence, the agreement, a limited power of attorney, payment directions, and identification, with notarization arranged for the documents [lLLfdrFLXFA @ 00:10:12]. Christopher opens differently: 'Hey Eric, hey, it's Chris,' then starts a conversation instead of leading with a company or service pitch. They emphasize questions about the person's situation [uhyVFTeepew @ 00:11:32]. Sean's Florida operation takes existing surplus leads into Excel, then Google Sheets, skip traces with services such as Skip Matrix or Skip Genie, and follows calls with voicemail, text, and mail. They print letters personally and describe reaching heirs before connecting them with their attorney [1uIxpXmBzuU @ 00:06:43]. BizMove offers another administrative stack: HubSpot CRM or Zoho CRM for contacts, follow-ups, and pipelines, plus AI-drafted follow-up messages [01plOr9pFjQ @ 00:04:32]. These are different implementations of the contact-and-follow-up work the speakers describe, from Sean's manually printed letters to Christopher's phone-first conversations and Richardson's evidence-backed introductory packet.

Price the fee and the work separately, as Richardson does in their $100,000 surplus illustration. A 30% success fee produces $30,000 before notary, filing, attorney, and mailing expenses. Their stated ranges are approximately $75–$100 for the notary, $75–$350 for filing, usually $1,500–$5,000 for attorney work depending on the case, and $50–$100 for FedEx. Attorneys may instead charge a third of the operator's fee or another negotiated structure [R8B06ovsDXI @ 00:17:03]. Shawn Bougie's probate recovery shows a different expense profile: a check slightly above $100,000, an owner share they recall agreeing at 50%, anticipated attorney costs of $10,000–$15,000, and estimated profit of $35,000–$40,000 before the researcher's share [fzvvdAGwCBM @ 00:01:11]. Payment routing is another explicit operating choice. Richardson describes assignment of interest, a payment-direction letter, or an attorney receiving and distributing funds. Where payment must go to the claimant, they describe an attorney escrow service taking $1,000 from the claim [R8B06ovsDXI @ 00:42:26]. Their earlier zero-money route instead has the claimant receive the check and pay a subsequent invoice through PayPal, with Richardson explicitly acknowledging the trust involved [1fbTnvEjC7M @ 00:05:27]. The fee agreement, expense allocation, and actual recipient of the check are separate parts of their deal structure.

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The launch order is a genuine disagreement. BizMove calls a professional website critical and proposes Wix ADI or Bookmark, AI-generated homepage copy, CRM automation, and a marketing plan as parts of the startup sequence [01plOr9pFjQ @ 00:03:52]. Taren attacks the familiar LLC, EIN, bank account, website, logo, and CRM checklist when it delays finding leads and making calls. Their claimed credibility comes from knowing the property, sale date, amount, and holder of funds, not the logo [8-8koApqnYA @ 00:05:10]. Nakia's mentorship pitch addresses the gap between information and execution through a 90-day, one-on-one action plan, process work, and building toward the participant's first $10,000 [c50hZiiw2FU @ 00:09:26]. Richardson offers a different support structure: self-directed course materials, a 90-day group program described as 12 weeks with four meetings weekly, and a business-setup option involving a team, CRM, virtual assistant, and CRM manager [lLLfdrFLXFA @ 00:17:11]. These speakers are not prescribing the same amount of infrastructure before outreach. Taren says the first call needs neither a website nor employees; BizMove makes online presentation part of the launch. Nakia emphasizes accountability and next actions, while Richardson's options range from learning independently to managing a prepared system and closing clients. The stated programs differ in delivery as well as in how much operating work remains with the beginner.

Marketing choices also differ in the practitioners' own results. Richardson ranks texting and calling highly, supports mailers, and calls door knocking 'undefeated,' recommending a company flyer, surplus details, supporting state law, and an agreement for the visit [R8B06ovsDXI @ 00:34:20]. Matthew says email has not worked for them and reminds them of scam pitches; their sequence is phone, text, letter, repeated through their Evernote workflow [vd__NHmQYgM @ 00:14:20]. Christopher reports postcard-generated inbound calls and says in-person marketing is not advantageous for their operation: they prefer making calls, including into other states, to driving between prospects [uhyVFTeepew @ 00:10:22]. Anthony's first California deal went the other way. After failed phone searches, social searches, neighbor contacts, and overnight letters, they located the auction buyer and drove to meet the former owner. Anthony reports a surplus of roughly $192,000 and a signed 35% fee after the in-person conversation [gB8lD75eL5I @ 00:05:20]. Anthony later describes calls, voicemail, text, and email as their regular approach rather than routine mailers. Door knocking was decisive in that difficult first case, while Christopher deliberately runs a phone-centered operation. Matthew's rejection of email is their reported experience, not the same ranking Richardson gives the channel or the sequence Anthony continues to use.

Deceased-owner files create another fork rather than one universal probate workflow. SurplusFundsRiches teaches reading the deed before chasing heirs, then comparing death and foreclosure dates. In their Barry-and-Elizabeth example, death before foreclosure transfers the interest under the stated survivorship arrangement, whereas death after foreclosure leaves an heirship issue for Barry's share [1N1Z99kUvRw @ 00:03:38]. Sean deliberately works leftover Florida claims that other operators avoid, often involving probate or someone outside the country. Their operation contacts heirs and uses an attorney found after calling approximately 12 attorneys about contingent work [1uIxpXmBzuU @ 00:08:56]. Bougie's partnership example shows a more layered probate structure: a local frontline attorney, a central attorney, a case manager, and a researcher receiving a share of net rather than the whole fee [fzvvdAGwCBM @ 00:00:18]. Matthew offers a different salvage route when a homeowner lead stalls: identify a judgment creditor and contract with that creditor as claimant. Fullmer reports actually recovering money through a defunct company's surviving connection after researching an old recorded judgment [vd__NHmQYgM @ 00:08:39]. The alternatives are therefore deed-based entitlement research, attorney-led heir claims, researcher partnerships, and creditor recovery. Matthew specifically distinguishes contracting with the creditor from taking assignment of the judgment, which they describe as potentially complex for someone unfamiliar with judgment work.

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Signed contracts and impressive recovery checks do not erase the payment gap. Fullmer recalls nearly returning to corrections work during their first year, despite eventually making about $118,000. They say 75% of that income arrived in the final quarter, and describe waits of three, four, or five months after signing. Matthew's approximately $60,000 is an expected result on contracted work, while their other businesses and investments provide an existing paycheck [vd__NHmQYgM @ 00:20:58]. Richardson similarly warns that working in July does not mean receiving payment in July. Their illustrative beginner economics use $5,000 for 60 hours, roughly $83 an hour, alongside an explicit warning that a specific monthly payment cannot be promised from court-driven timing [lFoZDRAGylo @ 00:01:02]. Anthony describes California tax-sale waiting as a year followed by additional months, depending on when the client is signed and when the sale occurred; that delay motivates interest in other states [gB8lD75eL5I @ 00:12:25]. Bougie's probate example also remains an estimate at the partner-payment stage: the check has reached the frontline attorney, but final attorney charges and net profit are not yet settled [fzvvdAGwCBM @ 00:01:29]. Each account distinguishes work completed, funds recovered, fee calculation, and actual cash received rather than treating a signed agreement as immediate income.

Anthony's first deal was not just finding a large number and collecting a signature. They could not find a working owner number, received no response from neighbors, and got nowhere with overnight letters. The auction buyer supplied the breakthrough, but the in-person visit uncovered another obstruction: the claimant had no ID, and the property had no phone service. Anthony drove back toward the freeway to arrange a notary, then later worked through the claimant's mother and sister to obtain identification. They paid for the sister's assistance and DMV paperwork before submission approximately a month and a half later [gB8lD75eL5I @ 00:09:40]. Matthew reports an agreement that had to be withdrawn because the claimant had forgotten another person was already working the case [vd__NHmQYgM @ 00:04:06]. Overage Acquisition describes that same duplicate-claim trap as wasted time, wasted budget, and an angry client; their check is the county's online portal or a call to the office before proceeding [bpxSOg1_xbE @ 00:02:05]. Richardson adds sale-status reversals: a bidder can fail to finish paying, a sale can be vacated, or bankruptcy can intervene after an initially attractive result [R8B06ovsDXI @ 00:26:24]. These operators describe missing documents, unreachable people, existing engagements, and changing sale status as concrete reasons a promising file does not immediately become a payable claim.

Growth exposes coordination work that the headline deal count leaves out. Sean reports about $300,000 recovered, $80,000 in success fees, and five to six hours of direct work per claim, but also says the business ran off and on for roughly a year and a half and that they hired a VA around active-duty scheduling constraints [1uIxpXmBzuU @ 00:04:24]. Richardson's later earnings overview describes that same success story as operating without employees, so the interview's staffing account and the later solo-business description do not match [lFoZDRAGylo @ 00:10:40]. Christopher supplies a different scaling sequence: admin first, then research capacity, then a case manager handling clients, notaries, and attorneys, before expanding sales. They explicitly reject pushing 100 deals through a broken process that fails to update claimants or follow trustees [uhyVFTeepew @ 00:08:05]. Bougie shows the coordination in one probate recovery: 46 back-and-forth emails involving the estate administrator, case management, updates, attorney liaison, and frontline attorney [fzvvdAGwCBM @ 00:00:35]. Sean's quoted claim hours, Christopher's division of work, and Bougie's email trail describe different operating arrangements. Christopher also admits that testing technology slowed their start; their growth account puts a functioning research and follow-up process before adding more salespeople to the front of it.

chapters.question_prompt: Where can I obtain free surplus lists, and how do I assemble leads when a county does not publish a usable list?
chapters.title: Find Free Lists and Build Your Own
chapters.subtitle: County websites, public records, Florida overbid lists, Texas list-building, mortgage-auction proceeds, and one-county specialization.
chapters.executive_summary: Free lists start with county searches, but the working lead comes from the records behind the list. Nicole, Bob Diamond, and Overage Acquisition teach county-and-state searches, downloadable reports, and direct requests. Florida demonstrations show three different jobs: filtering sold auctions, reading surplus PDFs, and retrieving ownership reports. Texas FundFinding builds a spreadsheet when a clerk says no list exists, then reduces preliminary proceeds for additional taxes. Alfred Taren puts manual sourcing and research at 10 to 20 hours weekly before calling. The strategic split is speed versus effort: public lists are accessible, self-built auction lists face less competition, and purchased research saves work. Mortgage bid gaps remain starting points; claim history, disbursements, liens, and county-specific instructions determine what deserves pursuit.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Start with the county, the state, and the money's local name. Bob Diamond searches for county-and-state overages or excess funds, then follows links labeled excess funds, overbids, or overages until a PDF or Excel spreadsheet appears. Their examples put the records with tax collectors, county treasurers, or sheriffs, rather than requiring a purchased lead service. Nicole at Next Level VA teaches the same basic route, but adds two exits when downloading fails: email the county or call its office. Nicole also adds PDF to the search phrase and substitutes a particular county for a broad statewide search. These are different ways to reach the same public-record starting point, not different kinds of recovered money. Overage Acquisition makes the search more specific with county, state, overage terminology, and year, demonstrating Fresno County, California, excess proceeds list 2023. Inside the county website, that demonstration follows property tax to tax sale and excess proceeds, then opens the available PDF. The shared instruction is practical: search for the jurisdiction and its sale records, follow the county's terminology, and request the material when the public page does not yield it. Diamond [4O5XeYwMAts @ 00:00:31]; Next Level VA [2e4YGOesnUY @ 00:14:16]; Overage Acquisition [6UiKunbtUa0 @ 00:01:10].

A usable surplus lead starts with a completed sale and identifiable property information, not simply a page headed unclaimed money. Nicole looks for tax deed numbers, parcel numbers, winning bids, estimated surplus, owner or business names, and sold dates. Some fields can be missing; the public-record research then supplies the owner and physical address needed for skip tracing. Nicole separates this work from lists of insurance proceeds or bank accounts that contain no real-estate identifiers. Alfred Taren likewise starts with a county tax deed surplus list containing sale dates, amounts, and property IDs, but points directly to the warning that available amounts can change. Taren then researches ownership, current location, and whether somebody has already filed. The Sumter County demonstration makes that distinction concrete: one record contains several owner-address lines, followed across the page by an application number, sale date, surplus amount, parcel number, and claim information. Its example currently shows no claims. Read the record as a property-and-sale entry rather than treating every displayed address as a separate opportunity. Across these approaches, the published list supplies identifiers and an amount to investigate; the records supply the missing people, property details, and claim status. Next Level VA [2e4YGOesnUY @ 00:12:31]; Alfred Taren [YCb5jYZX_A8 @ 00:01:10]; Tax Deed Surplus & Lien-Research Records [CFpu36h1xpA @ 00:00:21].

Learn how one county actually conducts sales before treating every foreclosure source as interchangeable. Eric Richardson at Money Making Juggernaut begins county specialization with upcoming sales and the location of sale results. Those results may sit on the county website or with Bid for Assets, Auction.com, Sales Web Civil View, or Zeus Auction. Richardson then moves to claim instructions and the claim form: what documents are requested, what the form asks, and how that county handles the work. Matt Joffrey at Surplus Funds Secrets adds a sourcing distinction: the same county can have mortgage-foreclosure and tax-sale lists in different corners, typically on different websites. Stopping after the first list can miss the second. Charlie at Surplus Systems follows the tax side through Google and emails to county departments, while preferring mortgage opportunities because they report less competition. For those, Charlie watches Auction.com and Realty.com and suggests contacting attorneys who start foreclosure proceedings to ask about lists. These practitioners share a county-first foundation without teaching one universal navigation path. Richardson's specialization means learning the local sales, results, forms, and research sources; Joffrey and Charlie show why that local map can contain more than one lead source. Money Making Juggernaut [FNbqvZGEzeE @ 00:00:38]; Surplus Funds Secrets [v0-thxE7IK4 @ 00:04:18]; Surplus Systems [dbTumm7HvnE @ 00:01:32].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: When the list is not posted, ask for the records in language the office can answer. Joffrey's email uses the subject Public Records Request, Surplus Funds Excess Proceeds List, addresses the records custodian, and requests the current unclaimed foreclosure and tax-sale surplus list, including case number, prior owner name, and amount held. The requested delivery is electronic if available, followed by the sender's name, email, and phone number. Joffrey says this is essentially what their office sends, including in counties without public lists. Overage Acquisition offers a shorter phone-or-email opening: ask for public records related to foreclosure surplus funds and ask how to access the list. The response may be the list itself, a portal, or instructions for a formal written request. Nicole's experienced-office approach is cordial rather than heavy-handed. When staff do not recognize the terminology, Nicole rephrases the request as surplus money from properties sold at foreclosure auction, or simply a list of properties sold at auction. The wording changes to fit the office's understanding; the requested sale records remain the target. Joffrey also reports that an office may ask the requester to separate tax overages from mortgage foreclosures. Surplus Funds Secrets [v0-thxE7IK4 @ 00:05:18]; Overage Acquisition [Tv7CWg8qUb0 @ 00:02:23]; Next Level VA [2e4YGOesnUY @ 00:16:19].

The Florida demonstrations turn an auction calendar into a working set of records. In Polk, Tax Deed Surplus & Lien-Research Records opens overbids, gets a sale date from the auction calendar, and selects May 18. Because the resulting view also includes later auctions, the demonstration filters the date column back to May 18 and the status column to sold. It then compares base bids with highest bids: $6,500 against $15,000, and $8,900 against $42,000. Opening View exposes the sale documents, with surplus letters or existing claims potentially under other documents. In Alachua, the same channel reports no online surplus list and instead opens a past auction date. The first filter is third-party bidder rather than certificate holder; the displayed example has a $644 opening bid and a $61,300 high bid. The next instruction is to download the property information report and examine mortgages or liens that may consume proceeds. Taren applies a related document-based method to court foreclosures: search the case number and retrieve the final judgment, certificate of sale, and certificate of disbursements. The documents establish debt, sale price, and what was paid out or remains. Tax Deed Surplus & Lien-Research Records [y94Ncg0WHn0 @ 00:01:10] [SGYpi5oeqOc @ 00:00:35]; Alfred Taren [YCb5jYZX_A8 @ 00:02:58].

Build the worksheet from the fields the sale and property records actually supply. Mark at Texas FundFinding uses Excel and begins with the auction date, later replacing it with the date the district clerk received the funds. Their other columns cover suit or case number, defendants, address, legal description, parcel number, sold price, minimum bid, additional taxes, and notes. The proceeds calculation uses sale price less minimum bid and other taxes owing, not the minimum bid alone. Nicole demonstrates a different Texas reconstruction in Tarrant: follow the account number into the tax assessor's payment history, open the receipt showing Tarrant County as payer, and note the former owner and $13,251.08 paid for taxes, penalties, interest, and attorney fees. Search that owner's name in the clerk's real-estate records, download the constable deed, and obtain the $41,000 sold price; Nicole reports $27,748.92 in surplus. Foreclose Houston supplies a mortgage-history alternative inside its login: select the county and sale month, choose sold to third parties, and submit the results. The displayed opening and final bids identify possible proceeds, and the service supports Excel export. These are three specific assembly methods, with different inputs and different research still to perform. Texas FundFinding [8UHfSY8oKfQ @ 00:00:56]; Next Level VA [2e4YGOesnUY @ 01:04:00]; Foreclose Houston [1s34X61MrsA @ 00:01:36].

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The practitioners do not agree that the easiest list is the best list to work. Diamond emphasizes how quickly Google produces free leads and describes lists as readily available inputs for contacting former owners. Nick Fullmer ranks the sourcing methods by effort and competition instead. Published lists are fast but the most competitive; requested lists remove some competitors who will not ask, while adding response delays and sometimes fees. Purchased lists deliver immediate access for money. Fullmer's favorite is creating lists by monitoring tax or foreclosure auctions, online or in person, because the extra work makes those leads less competitive. Overage Acquisition expresses the same auction-first preference and specifically reports getting business from Bid for Assets. Their method also uses Grant Street Group, where previous auctions appear under results. Neither auction advocate describes the work as disappearing: Fullmer explicitly calls time and effort the drawback of making your own list. Diamond's public-list route and Fullmer's self-built route therefore answer different operating preferences. One gets the operator to visible leads quickly; the other accepts more collection work in pursuit of less crowded opportunities. Diamond [4O5XeYwMAts @ 00:00:00]; Nick Fullmer- Overage Syndicate [HAQgKtwkxuE @ 00:07:54]; Overage Acquisition [6UiKunbtUa0 @ 00:05:08].

Free sourcing and paid convenience are presented side by side, not as mutually exclusive businesses. Joffrey challenges the idea that expensive special leads are necessary, saying the same county money and records can be reached without buying a list. Their office also sends records requests where nothing is posted, accepting the additional effort that others skip. Taren agrees that county lists and auctions are available but puts manual collection, court research, lien checks, and skip tracing at 10 to 20 hours weekly or more before calling. Taren's alternative is lead software delivering fresh, researched, vetted, and skip-traced files. Charlie at Surplus Systems also describes monthly list subscriptions as a way to speed up the process, but says the delivered leads still need skip tracing. That is a material difference in the service being described: Charlie's purchased list is not presented as the same finished product Taren promotes. The Sumter demonstrator offers another division of labor through Surplus Database: auction-day records, stored property information reports, and lien research at the pro subscription level. Keep those descriptions distinct when comparing the work a subscription replaces. Surplus Funds Secrets [v0-thxE7IK4 @ 00:00:00]; Alfred Taren [YCb5jYZX_A8 @ 00:05:10]; Surplus Systems [dbTumm7HvnE @ 00:01:18]; Tax Deed Surplus & Lien-Research Records [CFpu36h1xpA @ 00:01:42].

Mortgage bid gaps receive different treatment across the demonstrations. Foreclose Houston filters its mortgage-history database to third-party sales and compares opening with final bids, repeatedly calling the resulting opportunities possible or potential excess proceeds. One displayed comparison is an opening bid of $47,454 against a final bid described as 133.5. Eric Richardson is more forceful about the input: for mortgage foreclosures, do not trust the opening bid, which they say can be two-thirds of appraised value. Richardson instead looks for the final judgment or prayer amount in court documents. Taren separates the two mortgage routes. Judicial auctions use final judgments and sale results, followed by the case file; non-judicial platforms such as Auction.com and Xome provide opening and sold bids as a starting point. Taren says a large gap is not yet surplus because research still has to address mortgages, other liens, taxes, sale costs, and entitlement. The approaches overlap at finding candidates but diverge over how confidently the displayed bid difference can be used. Foreclose Houston's own possible-proceeds language fits that narrower candidate-search role rather than a completed determination of money available. Foreclose Houston [1s34X61MrsA @ 00:03:00]; Money Making Juggernaut [7oTjcr1c2u8 @ 00:06:04]; Alfred Taren [YCb5jYZX_A8 @ 00:03:26].

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Mark's Texas list-building starts with an actual refusal, not a hypothetical uncooperative office. A district clerk in a small South Texas county says the office does not have, sell, or maintain a list. Mark responds by assembling one from auction results and property records. The first proceeds figure in the worked example is $17,933, but Mark immediately questions taxes outside the foreclosure suit. They report that the collecting law firm regularly petitions to recover those additional taxes from the overage and has succeeded almost every time. Their hypothetical extra $4,000 is therefore added to the minimum bid when estimating total taxes, rather than assumed away. Mark later opens a May 2024 excess-proceeds filing and identifies the petitioner as the same party that forced the sale, seeking other taxes rather than acting as the homeowner. Nick Fullmer's example shows the same subtraction problem in a different form: after comparing $121,900 sold with a $6,692 opening bid, Fullmer deducts other fees and reports an approximate $102,978 overage. Both demonstrations move beyond the attractive first spread before presenting a working amount. Texas FundFinding [8UHfSY8oKfQ @ 00:00:17] [8UHfSY8oKfQ @ 00:06:40] [8UHfSY8oKfQ @ 00:11:13]; Nick Fullmer- Overage Syndicate [HAQgKtwkxuE @ 00:02:50].

Missing information can survive several clicks, and the practitioners show the workarounds they actually used. In Nicole's San Diego example, the assessor lookup supplies the property address but not the owner name; obtaining the deed there requires a purchase. Nicole instead opens the treasurer-tax collector's pay-bill search and uses the mailing address to obtain the name. Broward creates a different obstacle: the property-appraiser page has no historical-owner selection, so Nicole uses the records, taxes, and treasury site to find ownership for the relevant year. These are research bottlenecks encountered while completing specific lists, not reasons to assume the missing owner is unknowable. Marion's demonstration exposes another reading trap: multiple notification parties produce separate lines, but those lines link to the same document set. The demonstrator generates all eight pages of the ownership and encumbrance report and finds a mortgage with a book-and-page reference. Taren adds the broader workload consequence: manually checking county lists, calendars, court records, liens, and contact information can consume 10 to 20 hours weekly or more before any calling starts. Free acquisition does not remove the work those demonstrations require. Next Level VA [2e4YGOesnUY @ 00:51:09] [2e4YGOesnUY @ 00:55:04]; Tax Deed Surplus & Lien-Research Records [JP-3QXkQsUM @ 00:00:44]; Alfred Taren [YCb5jYZX_A8 @ 00:05:10].

Availability and recovery expense are separate checks from obtaining the list. Nicole warns that county publication can lag the auction and that stale lists may omit processed claims or leave too little time before filing deadlines. Their free checks include freshly released lists, asking whether the claimant signed with someone else, reviewing an available docket, and calling the office handling the overages. Richardson's one-county method distinguishes judicial case-number searches from non-judicial sales, where they instruct the operator to contact the trustee about claim status. Joffrey asks whether the office still holds the money, whether mortgages or liens remain unsatisfied, what filing deadline applies, and who can claim when an owner has died. Joffrey also reports request-response delays ranging from immediate replies to weeks, with some offices charging fees or mailing physical records. Diamond's economics introduce a later expense that free sourcing does not cover: their usual judicial-work budget is $2,500, while their administrative description uses a submitted form and a later check. Those are different recovery processes, not interchangeable cost assumptions. The operating checks remain the ones the practitioners name: current funds, existing claims, competing debts, the right claimant, and the actual recovery route. chapters.question_prompt: How do I verify an available surplus and research the debts and ownership records before contacting a claimant?
chapters.title: Verify the Surplus and Research Competing Debt
chapters.subtitle: Already-claimed funds, title searches, property liens, junior lienholders, claimant entitlement, and Florida county auction documents.
chapters.executive_summary: Eric Richardson, Alfred Taren, and Nick Fullmer agree that a surplus list is only the beginning: check existing claims, identify ownership, and research competing debt. Richardson uses county dockets, tax-deed portals, and recorder searches; Taren adds the foreclosure file, Propwire, the money holder, and current lienholder payoffs. Florida county walkthroughs show why document names and PDF update direction matter. Fullmer reports title-search prices around $100–$150; Richardson describes a wider $60–$500 range. Their approaches diverge on when to spend money and pursue uncertain files. Taren sometimes submits close cases to obtain the actual breakdown. Sade describes a more aggressive Texas owner-claim route when notified junior creditors fail to act, while explicitly retaining the possibility of later debt collection.

key_metrics.label: Already-filed application example
key_metrics.context: Richardson shows a surplus with an application already filed and says he would leave that case alone.

key_metrics.label: Fullmer's title-search price observation
key_metrics.context: Fullmer reports prices he found online while discussing alternatives for counties without online records.

key_metrics.label: Illustrated mortgage-surplus remainder
key_metrics.context: Taren's worked example subtracts a $95,000 second mortgage, $8,000 HOA debt, and $22,000 judgment from the listed surplus.

key_metrics.label: Undisclosed child-support lien
key_metrics.context: A speaker on Dustin Hahn's show recounts an early wholesale deal where the seller disclosed a $70,000 mortgage but omitted this lien.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The first agreement is blunt: a surplus figure does not tell you whether the file is still open for business or what the former owner can collect. Eric Richardson starts mortgage-foreclosure research with the civil case number, taken from the auction calendar or foreclosure information, and searches the county docket for an existing surplus claim. For tax-sale files, he checks a tax-deed portal or a county list; when neither supplies the answer, he calls or emails the county for unclaimed excess proceeds. Alfred Taren attacks the other half of the problem: the listed amount can already be spoken for by competing creditors, so he checks the actual case or sale file and what has already been paid. The Polk County demonstration makes both checks visible. Its results page shows a sold property and a $45,000 surplus balance, but the researcher still opens the documents tab for claims and the disbursement tab for remaining funds. Richardson's application-status examples also distinguish an application, denial, appeal, and payment rather than treating the dollar amount as the whole story. These practitioners work through the file, not merely through the headline number on a list. Money Making Juggernaut [ZU8-PRxVeCg @ 00:00:39]; Alfred Taren [SzfjJzM76ls @ 00:04:17]; Tax Deed Surplus & Lien-Research Records [C9X-hGZ_2bI @ 00:00:26].

The second agreement is that competing debt has to be researched before treating surplus as the owner's payout. Taren describes second mortgages, home-equity lines, HOA claims, judgments, tax liens, and city charges as recurring items. On the mortgage-foreclosure side, his sequence is the foreclosing lender, later liens in order, and then the owner; a loan recorded before the foreclosing loan usually stays with the house rather than drawing from that surplus. On the tax-sale side, he explains that removing a lien from the house can move the creditor's claim over to the money. Sade gives the same basic distinction in a Texas illustration: the tax sale removes the collateral, but the mortgage debt remains, and the lender can seek excess proceeds. Dave at Private Investigator Videos adds that dates alone are not the entire title analysis: government claims, municipal claims, and certain priority liens can behave differently. AFX Research's Texas search route therefore reaches beyond mortgages into tax records, judgments, and commercial UCC filings. None of these speakers reduces the work to spotting the word 'mortgage' and subtracting one recorded figure. Their recurring subjects are the sale type, recording history, creditor priority, and what debt actually remains. Alfred Taren [LdemHPCk0dk @ 00:01:10]; SadeLegal Law Firm [rNxycxH3ATc @ 00:01:08]; Private Investigator Videos [GWuQIN0aSwQ @ 00:00:50]; AFX Research LLC [HPyO3dkjbCQ @ 00:01:49].

Ownership research is the other baseline prerequisite, and the speakers make it more specific than finding a name beside an address. Nick Fullmer says to confirm who owned the property at the time of sale and, in certain states, who was on the mortgage. He singles out Minnesota as a place where, in his account, the surplus belongs to the mortgagor rather than necessarily the person named on the deed. Richardson's county-recorder method begins with the previous owner's name, because that is how he searches recorded liens and then checks the asset tied to each document. Dustin Hahn's show demonstrates another ownership problem: someone claiming to own the whole property may have another person on title, or may actually be another wholesaler. The panel uses county records to expose those mismatches before a contract reaches the title company. Taren adds deceased-owner files to the picture. He says the right to the funds can pass to family, with relationship or heirship evidence and sometimes probate, and suggests an obituary or skip trace to locate them. The practical agreement is to establish whose interest you are researching before presenting a potential recovery to the person who answers the phone. Nick Fullmer- Overage Syndicate [KOYBZFn2k7w @ 00:01:15]; Money Making Juggernaut [q95klfFm9mE @ 00:02:04]; Dustin Hahn [6IAi_pcEgFY @ 00:04:48]; Alfred Taren [SzfjJzM76ls @ 00:03:24].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Richardson's inexpensive lien search starts with a county-provided property information report or owner's and encumbrance report. He says these identify the title holder, liens, and book-and-page references for recorded documents. Without that report, he searches the county recorder under the previous owner's name, then opens the deed and lien documents. Taren starts even closer to the foreclosure: in a court case, the parties named in the lawsuit can reveal other lienholders, and the final judgment usually includes the bank's interest and fees. For a trustee sale, he starts with the notice of sale. He uses NETR Online as a directory to county recording offices and Propwire as a free property-data starting point, while calling its balances estimates. AFX Research separates Texas searches by office: county clerk for recorded property documents, tax assessor-collector for unpaid property taxes, district or county clerk for judgments, and Secretary of State for commercial UCC filings. Rent Own Sell supplies another paid-data option, PropertyShark, and says title companies can perform lien searches for a fee. These are the actual routes the speakers name; the county report, recorded instrument, and estimated property-data balance serve different jobs in their research. Money Making Juggernaut [q95klfFm9mE @ 00:00:53]; Alfred Taren [LdemHPCk0dk @ 00:03:03]; AFX Research LLC [HPyO3dkjbCQ @ 00:01:09]; Rent Own Sell [VBvaq5etzV4 @ 00:01:23].

The Florida walkthroughs turn Richardson's report-and-records method into county-specific clicks. In Polk, search the tax-deed number, confirm sold rather than redeemed, and open the property information report. Its owner-information area supplies the deed's book and page; the official records search retrieves the deed. Notification addresses sit under NOA party labels, not simply NOA parties. Miami-Dade also takes the tax-deed number, but its results page does not display available surplus. The researcher opens the documents and surplus letter, then finds a title search on the last page. That report lists two deed references, which the demonstration follows to a warranty deed and a quitclaim deed. Notification addresses appear under Comm parties, and the tax-deed certification is labeled DR513. Citrus nests the property information report inside the application. Its owner section again supplies book and page, while notification addresses are called letters clerk's affidavit. Citrus also updates the surplus-notice file with later claim materials, so the researcher scrolls beyond blank forms into submitted documents. Richardson describes book-and-page references as the route to the official record; these county examples show where those references and related claim materials actually appear. Tax Deed Surplus & Lien-Research Records [C9X-hGZ_2bI @ 00:01:26]; Tax Deed Surplus & Lien-Research Records [sschUpuRZoU @ 00:01:37]; Tax Deed Surplus & Lien-Research Records [bmmWj7_LTrw @ 00:01:25]; Money Making Juggernaut [q95klfFm9mE @ 00:01:06].

The remaining Florida examples require a different scrolling strategy, not a different objective. Volusia puts the documents into one large PDF and adds incoming claims at the top. The demonstration searches by auction date, uses Control-F to locate the entry, and then finds the surplus notice, certificate of mailing, application, and property report. The deed comes from the report's owner-information book-and-page reference. Leon places the title search inside a document labeled with a year-like number; the opening page is an order form, so the researcher scrolls to the report and finds the owner's quitclaim deed in the same document. Leon's notification addresses come from the case's parties tab rather than a separate address document. Escambia requires the auction date and tax-deed number, opens its combined PDF through a magnifying-glass icon, and appends new documents at the end. Its surplus notice therefore appears toward the bottom. Fullmer supplies the fallback when a county offers no online documents at all: ask the recorder about a one-off search, pay a local researcher, or order a title search. He names Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, and real-estate groups as places to find somebody who can visit the recorder's office. sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest contrast is not whether junior creditors exist, but what happens when they do not act. Taren's baseline is that the former owner stands behind qualifying creditors, yet he also says missed filing deadlines can move more money to the owner. Richardson makes a more specific Florida timing claim: he describes 120 days on the tax-sale side after the notice notification and 60 days on the mortgage-foreclosure side, while telling viewers to ask the county about the applicable period. Sade develops a more aggressive Texas owner-claim illustration. With $190,000 in excess proceeds and a $100,000 mortgage, the ordinary split in the example is $100,000 to the lender and $90,000 to the owner. Sade says the owner can pursue all the excess if the required procedural steps and notices are followed and the lender fails to intervene. That does not erase Sade's separate warning about the surviving debt: the lender can pursue a personal judgment, and Sade discusses bankruptcy or negotiating a smaller settlement as possible responses. The contrast is a creditor-payment baseline versus an owner pursuing funds after creditor inaction, not an assertion that every tax sale automatically cancels every debt. Alfred Taren [SzfjJzM76ls @ 00:03:05]; Money Making Juggernaut [q95klfFm9mE @ 00:03:28]; SadeLegal Law Firm [rNxycxH3ATc @ 00:02:39]; SadeLegal Law Firm [rNxycxH3ATc @ 00:05:33].

The research budget has several competing playbooks, and the quoted prices are not uniform. Richardson describes county reports and recorder searches as the easy, inexpensive route, then puts paid title searches anywhere from $60 to $300–$500. Fullmer reports finding searches around $100–$150 online and calls that expensive for the obstacle he is discussing. Rather than presenting a paid report as the only answer, he offers a local researcher, a recorder willing to help on a single case, or a local title-company referral that might produce a better rate. Rent Own Sell adds PropertyShark as an address-based third-party search for a nominal fee and notes that title companies can also supply buyer history. AFX Research emphasizes the broader professional-search job: a full chain of title, possible ownership gaps, easements, and covenants alongside liens. The scope is therefore different as well as the price. Richardson is teaching surplus-related lien discovery; AFX is describing title review for purchasers, investors, and lenders. Fullmer's cost discussion concerns getting unavailable local records. Those figures and methods sit side by side as attributed options, rather than collapsing into one supposedly standard price or one universal search package. Money Making Juggernaut [q95klfFm9mE @ 00:03:00]; Nick Fullmer- Overage Syndicate [KOYBZFn2k7w @ 00:04:29]; Rent Own Sell [VBvaq5etzV4 @ 00:01:38]; AFX Research LLC [HPyO3dkjbCQ @ 00:02:24].

The speakers also draw different lines around imperfect information. Richardson shows a $47,000 surplus with an application already filed and says he would leave it alone. Taren describes a different situation: a file where competing debt leaves the likely owner remainder uncertain. He does not always discard that file. He tells the homeowner it costs nothing to take a look, submits the claim, and asks for an itemized breakdown; the real answer arrives with lienholder payoffs. These are alternative responses to different obstacles, not conflicting instructions about the same case. Dave's title-search approach is firmer about the evidence used to understand the property: inspect the official title abstract rather than accepting the auction company's or owner's word. Taren still uses owner conversations to fill gaps, asking whether a recorded debt was paid, what the last payoff showed, and how far behind the owner was. Sade's aggressive claim discussion similarly separates a possible outcome from effortless execution: Sade describes repeated notices, chances for intervention, and substantial courtroom work. Across these approaches, the dividing questions are whether someone already filed, whether the remaining amount is merely uncertain, and whether the contemplated claim requires a contested procedural fight. Money Making Juggernaut [ZU8-PRxVeCg @ 00:03:15]; Alfred Taren [LdemHPCk0dk @ 00:06:09]; Private Investigator Videos [GWuQIN0aSwQ @ 00:02:29]; SadeLegal Law Firm [rNxycxH3ATc @ 00:07:18].

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The clearest firsthand economics reversal comes from Dustin Hahn's wholesale panel, not from a surplus-recovery payout. A speaker recounts an early deal where the seller reported a $70,000 mortgage. The speaker considered contracting at $100,000 and wholesaling at roughly $120,000, expecting about $20,000. The title company then uncovered a $30,000 child-support lien the seller had omitted, changing the deal. The panel also reports sellers forgetting second mortgages and contracts arriving without every person on title involved. Taren supplies the surplus-recovery version of the bottleneck: files have sat for months because one lienholder had not sent a payoff. Some liens later turn out not to exist anymore, increasing the potential remainder; other files shrink when the actual debt comes back. These accounts are different from Taren's explicit arithmetic illustrations. His $180,000 example falls to $55,000 after the stated second mortgage, HOA debt, and judgment; his $60,000 tax-surplus example produces nothing for an owner facing a $70,000 mortgage claim. The firsthand lesson is hidden debt and delayed payoffs; the worked examples show the economic direction without pretending they are completed recoveries or measured average results. Dustin Hahn [6IAi_pcEgFY @ 00:00:55]; Alfred Taren [LdemHPCk0dk @ 00:06:24]; Alfred Taren [SzfjJzM76ls @ 00:01:26].

Fullmer's demonstrated obstacle is a recorded Medicaid-related lien renewal with no dollar amount. The record confirms an interest but does not answer the question he needs answered: how much competing debt exists. He points to Healthcare and Family Services in Chicago on the document and recommends calling the recording entity with the case number or address to ask whether the lien remains outstanding and what it totals. Taren explains another reason a visible amount can mislead. Interest, penalties, fees, and lender advances for taxes or insurance can accumulate while public records lag; human data entry can introduce errors as well. His money-holder call establishes what is being held, not today's second-mortgage or HOA payoff. AFX Research supplies the reverse problem: a debt may have been paid without the lien ever being officially released. Its response is to contact the lienholder and ensure a release is filed once the matter is resolved. Dave adds that lien age, priority, and possible negotiation deserve inspection rather than assumptions. Together, these speakers identify missing amounts, stale amounts, and unreleased instruments as separate research problems. A document can be real while the economic conclusion drawn from its face is still wrong. Nick Fullmer- Overage Syndicate [KOYBZFn2k7w @ 00:03:02]; Alfred Taren [LdemHPCk0dk @ 00:04:17]; AFX Research LLC [HPyO3dkjbCQ @ 00:02:44]; Private Investigator Videos [GWuQIN0aSwQ @ 00:01:22].

The document walkthroughs expose small navigation failures with direct consequences for what the researcher sees. In Polk, the presenter opens NOA parties, fails to find the expected addresses, and corrects the choice to NOA party labels. Miami-Dade's surplus letter shows an original $233,356, but the researcher also identifies claims from Royal Properties and Miami Florida Home Solutions. That is an original-surplus figure accompanied by competing filings, not a displayed owner payout. Richardson's own examples make the same distinction with a $47,000 surplus he would leave alone because an application was already filed. Taren's closing warning addresses what happens if research shortcuts reach the phone call: say 'possible funds' or 'estimated surplus,' and do not promise a number. He has seen the actual remainder move in both directions after lien information arrives. The county demonstrations also show why the operator needs the document itself: a label can lead to the wrong notification material, while an earlier surplus letter can sit beside later claims. The money displayed, the documents submitted, and the amount ultimately left for the claimant are different facts in these practitioners' examples. Their checks keep those facts separate instead of turning an attractive list entry into a promised recovery. Read the foreclosure file or trustee-sale notice, then search recorded mortgages, liens, and judgments; use NETR Online to locate the county recording office. [Alfred Taren — LdemHPCk0dk @ 00:03:03]

Call the entity that recorded a lien when the document omits its amount; ask whether the lien is still outstanding and how much it is for. [Nick Fullmer- Overage Syndicate — KOYBZFn2k7w @ 00:03:47]

Ask the clerk, trustee, or county how much money is held, and obtain current competing balances from the relevant lienholders rather than treating the held balance as the owner's remainder. [Alfred Taren — LdemHPCk0dk @ 00:04:51]

chapters.question_prompt: How does mortgage-foreclosure surplus recovery differ from tax-sale recovery, and what do the jurisdiction-specific examples show?
chapters.title: Mortgage Foreclosures and Sheriff-Sale Recovery
chapters.subtitle: Judicial and nonjudicial sales, PropertyRadar research, Texas and Georgia workflows, California and New Jersey guidance, and Philadelphia sheriff auctions.
chapters.executive_summary: Chuck Panzarella, Bob Diamond, Josh Sternberg, and Lawrence Friscia agree that foreclosure can leave money for former owners, but debt, competing liens, and claim procedures determine what reaches them. Eric Richardson separates county-held judicial cases from trustee-held nonjudicial recoveries, using auction.com, PropertyRadar, and Excess Elite for research and outreach. His Texas example produced a $16,609 check request and a 30% success fee; his Georgia workflow checks auction results against debt records. Diamond reports charging 30–40%, while David Church describes 10–30%. Practitioners differ over attorney involvement and payout speed. New Jersey examples emphasize priority and service; Philadelphia auction operators and lawyers describe settlement deadlines, title exposure, and litigation that can interrupt a sale.
