sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The common starting point is money left after the foreclosure debt is paid, not the fact that a house changed hands. Chuck Panzarella of Consumer Action Law Group illustrates the basic spread with a $300,000 loan and a $500,000 sale, leaving $200,000; reversing those figures leaves nothing to claim. Their actual verification sequence goes beyond that simple example: establish ownership through title, examine foreclosure records, and subtract the liens or loans paid at the sale [gUeG4eQdMy8 @ 00:01:24]. Josh Sternberg makes the additional debt visible in a California example: a $400,000 first mortgage, $100,000 second mortgage, and $50,000 tax lien total $550,000 against a $750,000 winning bid. The resulting $200,000 is what remains after those payoffs, not after the first mortgage alone [z6jQuGWdtDY @ 00:01:19]. Lawrence Friscia gives the New Jersey version: a $280,000 judgment and $340,000 sale create $60,000 in surplus, but the former owner does not receive an automatic payment [i8-qVMepHe8 @ 00:00:48]. These practitioners put the arithmetic beside ownership and payment procedure. Panzarella asks for proof of ownership; Sternberg works through the liens; Friscia distinguishes a surplus from an automatic check. Their examples all begin with a sale that actually brings in more than the stated debt.

The business itself is finding the money, reaching the person connected to it, and moving a claim through the relevant process. Hutch & Holmes names that sequence directly: find, inform, assist. Their starting assignment is to choose one state, establish what service the business will provide, and understand the filing process before chasing leads [L2oKpjOoh20 @ 00:00:36]. Bob Diamond describes the commercial version through a court registry list. The list can contain mortgage overages alongside appellate bonds and support payments, so their team picks out lender-versus-person cases, follows the docket number, and identifies the former owners. The outreach then offers help recovering identified money for a percentage [lzU09FRqmhg @ 00:01:27]. David Church explains why that contact can matter: former owners have moved, a mailer arrives weeks later, and they do not know money remains. Their service prepares the paperwork and helps claim it [k0pvzqTug-M @ 00:00:44]. County Assets Recovery similarly describes pulling county records, identifying the rightful owner, building a documented claim, and handling filing and follow-up [siNLN4gsAEA @ 00:00:30]. Across these approaches, the service is not simply handing somebody a list. The speakers describe locating the claimant, explaining the recovery, assembling documents, and staying with the claim through the holder's process.

The first operational split is where the sale and its money are handled. Eric Richardson describes judicial mortgage foreclosures as county or sheriff matters with a civil case, a docket, and records that can show claims, disbursements, or excess proceeds. Their nonjudicial route instead leads to a trustee, often a law firm or large company, that conducts the sale and handles the money [kYJAnAiPgvc @ 00:00:39]. Diamond's mortgage workflow starts later, after the foreclosing creditor and other required items are paid and the excess is deposited with the court. Their research target is the clerk's registry, followed by the individual case [lzU09FRqmhg @ 00:00:39]. Panzarella describes contacting the sale trustee and submitting a claim either to that trustee or to the court, noting that funds are generally deposited with the court after two or three months [gUeG4eQdMy8 @ 00:01:47]. The shared prerequisite is identifying the holder and the claim route, rather than treating every foreclosure as a county claim form. Richardson asks the trustee for a disbursement breakdown and its own claim form. Diamond uses the case number to reach the details behind a registry entry. Panzarella connects title and sale verification to the trustee before describing possible hearings and motions. Each route starts with records and ends with a specific claim process.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Richardson's Georgia mortgage workflow begins before the first-Tuesday sale. Create a free auction.com account, select Georgia and foreclosure homes, and heart the properties before the auction so the sale-result emails arrive afterward. Their instruction explicitly excludes bank-owned properties from that search [FJj3hN2KbIg @ 00:08:50]. For a property reported sold to a third-party bidder, Richardson opens foreclosure contact information to identify the attorney or trustee. They then use a free foreclosurebidlist.com account, select the county, and open the property report. In their worked example, the email reports a $427,000 sale, auction.com shows an opening bid around $185,661, and the second report shows a $179,281 remaining balance. Richardson uses the higher number, saying it could include additional interest and foreclosure fees [FJj3hN2KbIg @ 00:10:41]. This research sequence serves the same verification task Panzarella identifies: use foreclosure records to establish funds after loans and liens paid at the sale [gUeG4eQdMy8 @ 00:01:24]. Richardson continues with lien research and additional-mortgage checks rather than stopping at the auction spread. Their example shows a home equity line that was released. After the client signs an agreement, they contact the foreclosure attorney holding the money to verify the surplus and obtain the details needed to pursue it.

PropertyRadar is Richardson's research tool for the nonjudicial information gap. They say auction.com removes trustee information after foreclosure and that sale prices require the email notification, while PropertyRadar lets them retrieve trustee details later [XNxo6xvEJBg @ 00:01:13]. Their property report review covers deed transfers, purchases, loans, liens, transaction histories, and book-and-page references; some documents can also be pulled directly. Although the platform includes skip tracing and contact functions, Richardson says they use Excess Elite for those activities and PropertyRadar for due diligence and trustee identification. They also describe preforeclosure lists and alerts for properties sold to third-party bidders above the published bid. Their most expensive package is recalled as about $200 or $300 monthly, while basic research can use a basic plan [XNxo6xvEJBg @ 00:04:33]. Diamond describes a different research engine: request registry deposits, inspect the lender-versus-owner case, and use the docket to recover full party details [lzU09FRqmhg @ 00:01:55]. The two workflows put different records at the center. Richardson needs the private sale handler's identity and the property's debt history; Diamond needs the court deposit and its case. Both move from an initial lead to the documents and people behind the money before describing a completed recovery.

The Texas case supplies Richardson's concrete execution sequence. A student, Joanne, brought a single-family-home lead from Excess Elite; the research checked the sale against mortgage debt and looked for additional obligations. The owners were divorced, so the recovery had to be split, and Richardson says the initially identified surplus was higher. Their first contact was an introductory email with proof, followed by an agreement sent through Rabbit Sign [7AHHRIbWG80 @ 00:02:05]. With the agreement signed, they contacted the trustee, attached that agreement, requested confirmation and a claim form, and supplied the requested company representation letter. The response authorized a $16,609 check request. Richardson reports correspondence from September 9 to September 11, with the check arriving September 12, and less than two hours of work [7AHHRIbWG80 @ 00:03:09]. Their reported 30% fee produced a little less than $5,000. Diamond's court route uses a different document: an attorney-prepared petition telling the sale story, the amount owed, the selling price, and the former owner's request for payment. They describe these petitions as usually six or seven paragraphs [lzU09FRqmhg @ 00:03:07]. sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Attorney involvement is where the operating models visibly diverge. Diamond's service signs the client and brings in an attorney to petition for court-held money; their reason is that the recovery operator cannot represent someone else in court [lzU09FRqmhg @ 00:03:25]. Leonard Boyer of Lenny the Lawyer-Live takes a more specialist-centered position in New Jersey, describing precise, technical proceedings and saying this is not something just any attorney handles [dn1b-e6bUyo @ 00:01:13]. Richardson, by contrast, says the Texas case was completed without an attorney on their side. They distinguish a living homeowner's straightforward claim form from a legal motion or filing and describe their role as limited-power-of-attorney representation for inquiry, confirmation, and paperwork [7AHHRIbWG80 @ 00:04:14]. Hutch & Holmes makes the service boundary the first business-design question: determine how a claimant files without an attorney, what documents are required, where the claim goes, what fee and contract rules apply, and when legal work requires an attorney [L2oKpjOoh20 @ 00:01:52]. These are different workflows, not interchangeable instructions. Diamond is describing a court petition for another person; Richardson is describing the trustee's accepted paperwork in one completed Texas case. Hutch & Holmes also explicitly says notary status does not confer authority to represent someone in court.

There is no single payout clock in the practitioners' accounts. Diamond describes their mortgage recovery process as usually three or four months after the client is signed and an attorney petitions for release [lzU09FRqmhg @ 00:05:29]. Richardson reports the Texas trustee inquiry producing a check cut within three days, with the case's correspondence and delivery dates illustrating that fast turnaround [7AHHRIbWG80 @ 00:00:55]. Yet Richardson's broader mortgage-versus-tax comparison says judicial mortgage payouts have typically been faster in their experience because a motion reaches a court date, whereas nonjudicial trustees sometimes drag their feet [ZJ74a_7vvzo @ 00:05:46]. Their separate judicial comparison also says some trustees pay faster than counties and may withhold information until 30 or even 60 days after sale. Fees vary just as visibly. Diamond reports charging 30–40%, leaving 60–70% for the former owner. David Church instead describes a 10–30% sliding scale and says very small recoveries may carry a higher percentage [k0pvzqTug-M @ 00:00:57]. The Texas example's 30% fee is a reported case outcome, while Diamond and Church describe their broader pricing practices. The speakers supply both quick trustee payments and slower trustee behavior, alongside a separate months-long court workflow. Their accounts do not settle on one universal speed advantage.

Sheriff sale is not a sufficient label for deciding whether the underlying matter is tax or mortgage. Richardson says to inspect the plaintiff: a county treasurer points toward a tax sale, while a bank points toward mortgage foreclosure [ZJ74a_7vvzo @ 00:03:01]. Philadelphia makes that distinction tangible. Shawn at bid4assets says the platform hosts both tax and mortgage foreclosure auctions for the sheriff, then gives a buyer workflow specifically for tax delinquent and tax lien auctions. Their settlement explanation gives winning bidders until the next business day's close to fund the remainder of 10% of the winning bid plus the 10% buyer's premium, followed by 15 days from auction close to fund the remaining balance [1BmnpBQHhAY @ 00:16:21]. Console Matison LLP describes Philadelphia clients missing a 10-day balance-payment period after a 10% deposit and pursuing litigation to complete the sale [7eeXOhOafjc @ 00:04:12]. Those stated payment windows differ. The platform walkthrough directs bidders to the settlement terms on the sale and individual auction pages; the law firm's account addresses a failed completion and a motion to rescue it. Both concern purchasers' auction obligations, while Richardson's plaintiff check concerns classifying a surplus lead. Neither Philadelphia buyer workflow is presented as a former owner's surplus-claim form.

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Richardson's first mortgage-specific trap is treating the opening bid as the debt. They say it can instead be two-thirds of an appraisal, two-thirds of a final judgment, or an amount chosen by the trustee. Their remedy is finding the final judgment or final writ and reviewing the actual amount due [0pjP-Sr15PA @ 00:00:39]. Their next trap is accepting a statement that another creditor swallowed the surplus without checking payment. Richardson requests disbursement history because entitlement alone does not establish that the trustee actually paid that creditor. They ask what happens to the money if the entitled party never claimed it [0pjP-Sr15PA @ 00:02:30]. Sternberg adds two California distinctions. A property reverting to the bank as REO produces no surplus in their explanation because no winning third-party bidder supplied sale money. A second-mortgage foreclosure is different again: the first mortgage remains, and Sternberg says the former owner's debt requires attention even after ownership is lost [z6jQuGWdtDY @ 00:01:57]. Boyer likewise warns that selling above the mortgage balance does not settle availability because other creditors may be owed money [dn1b-e6bUyo @ 00:02:37]. These are the speakers' checks against a misleading gross spread: actual judgment, actual disbursements, the identity of the buyer, and the position of the foreclosing debt.

The file can also fail after money has been identified. Friscia names four recurring New Jersey problems: not serving every party, missing a lien whose holder then objects, lacking authority for a deceased owner's estate, and proposing amounts that do not match the court's records. The last problem can produce a rejected order; all four can delay payment [i8-qVMepHe8 @ 00:02:30]. Their estate explanation says the family usually needs authority from the Surrogate, while remaining funds belong to the former owner only after valid junior liens are addressed [i8-qVMepHe8 @ 00:01:24]. Richardson's Georgia research encounters a different dead end: existing excess-funds lists may include claims already made, and only some counties flag pending claims. They ask prospects whether somebody has contacted them or whether a claim has already been submitted, then use available court records to investigate [FJj3hN2KbIg @ 00:04:38]. County Assets Recovery warns about money eventually moving to the state, whereas Friscia says New Jersey's motion rule sets no fixed deadline but waiting risks competing claims, harder-to-find records, and eventual state transfer [siNLN4gsAEA @ 00:00:30]. The concrete bottlenecks are missing service, missing authority, missing liens, mismatched amounts, and an already-active claim—not simply whether a lead list displays a large dollar figure beside a name.

Philadelphia's buyer-side accounts show failures that occur around completion of the sale itself. Console Matison LLP reports seeing post-sale litigation at their office, including redemption attempts that can leave a purchaser seeking their money back from the city [7eeXOhOafjc @ 00:02:14]. Their clients also encounter missing tax-clearance certificates and missed balance payments. The described rescue route begins with intervention in the underlying case under Pennsylvania Rule of Civil Procedure 2327, then a motion to complete the sheriff sale; the firm says an LLC needs a lawyer for that filing [7eeXOhOafjc @ 00:04:57]. Shawn's bid4assets walkthrough separately warns that failure to meet settlement terms means default and deposit forfeiture. Their bidder-on-deck process can offer the property to the next-highest bidder, who has 24 hours to accept and 15 days from acceptance to pay [1BmnpBQHhAY @ 00:13:42]. Recovery economics have their own bottleneck: Diamond calls signing people up the hardest part, emphasizing natural skepticism and the time needed to find people willing to accept help [lzU09FRqmhg @ 00:06:30]. The firsthand reports therefore include stalled purchases and stalled client acquisition, not just paperwork. Diamond's reported fee range sits alongside that sales work; the Philadelphia accounts place litigation and lost deposits beside the appeal of auction discounts.

chapters.question_prompt: How do I pursue a recovery when the claimant is difficult to locate, is a company, lives overseas, or has died?
chapters.title: Difficult Claimants, Heirs, and Estate Cases
chapters.subtitle: Company lookups, deceased-owner skip tracing, heir outreach, probate questions, overseas recovery, and deaths during an active claim.
chapters.executive_summary: Death, stale addresses, dissolved companies, and overseas ownership change the recovery work; they do not automatically end it. Whitman starts company research with state business records, while Church and Fullmer pursue relatives, obituaries, and family trees. Pierce Law Group separates estate authority from an heir's eventual distribution. Danielle reports completing an overseas recovery through WhatsApp, Google Translate, and translated notarizations, negotiating a 20% fee after back taxes reduced the funds to $87,000. The playbooks diverge on probate appetite, outreach sequencing, fees, and even the California affidavit threshold quoted by Overage Acquisition. Church's unsigned paperwork, Fullmer's missing obituary, and Bucci's claimant dying before final documentation expose the bottlenecks behind apparently straightforward recoveries.

key_metrics.label: Overseas recovery after back taxes
key_metrics.context: Danielle reports that back taxes reduced the overseas owner's recovery from $97,000 to $87,000; the reduction preceded the fee discussion.

key_metrics.label: Separate deceased unmarried owners

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The shared starting point is that a death changes the contact and claim path rather than automatically destroying the recovery. Bob Diamond describes a student whose claimant died unexpectedly while a deal was progressing. Their response is to open the skip-trace report, identify first-degree relatives, and telephone the surviving spouse or descendants instead of treating the file as finished. William Whitman makes a different part of the same distinction: the deceased individual cannot make the claim, but the estate can. Overages Overflow likewise describes tax-sale surplus as usually becoming part of the deceased owner's estate, with heirs needing to establish that they are the right people. That channel also explains why heirs may know nothing about the money: notices go to the owner's last known address, which may now be empty, sold, or occupied by someone else. These practitioners therefore keep the recovery alive while changing whom they pursue and what authority they establish. Diamond's immediate work is locating living family; Whitman's is identifying the estate that can claim; Overages Overflow's is asking the holding office whether excess funds exist rather than waiting for a notice to arrive. [ohOWpmEzDmA @ 00:00:13] [JRxMS-A2mXQ @ 00:00:40] [XTbc1Dz6dxY @ 00:00:16]

The baseline research also separates finding a relative from establishing who can actually move the file. Surplus Systems tells operators to return to the original case before buying skip tracing: verify the property, ownership, case, and person who may have the claim. A familiar surname is a clue, not automatic entitlement. Nick Fullmer asks whether a will exists because that answer changes how they proceed and how the overage is distributed. Their practical organizing tool is a drawn family tree. In one active case, an apparent eight-child estate became a different research problem when they established that all eight children had died and identified roughly four heirs further down the family. Pierce Law Group places formal claim authority with the estate's qualified personal representative in most North Carolina reverse-mortgage estate cases. That representative requests release from the clerk and supplies evidence of authority tied to the foreclosure file. Together, these accounts distinguish the contact list, the family picture, and the person presenting the estate's request. Fullmer's tree explains whom they are investigating; Pierce's representative supplies authority; Surplus Systems keeps the entire search anchored to the original property and case rather than to a name alone. [RPpdYzSL6jE @ 00:00:49] [zUGQVkbDEzc @ 00:03:43] [ErS3fgilrDY @ 00:00:33]

Practitioners also agree on preparing the family conversation with specific information instead of a vague promise of found money. Overage Acquisition starts with an obituary search and the survivor section, collecting names and cities before calling. David Church's live insurance-account call shows why that preparation matters: the person answering was not the person Church expected, and the family had shifted estate responsibilities toward another relative. Church asked who had been in charge, whether copies of the will or trust existed, and who could proceed. Looking back, they criticize their own repeated filler words and attempts to sell the company instead of letting the account details carry the conversation. People Locator Skip Tracing supplies another research route: probate filings in the county where a deceased relative lived, with a filed will naming beneficiaries. Their search guidance also follows relatives across states where they lived or worked because distributions can be returned from outdated addresses. Across these approaches, the preparation is concrete: family names, locations, account or property details, and existing estate documents. Church's conversation then moves toward the person with the ability to sign, rather than assuming the first helpful family member is the final contact. [6vsHnTS609Y @ 00:00:46] [VGzK7EytsBw @ 00:03:01] [mZfLBxhYGpw @ 00:01:00]

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: For company claimants, Whitman's demonstration begins with the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau's December 2022 sale disbursement check register. They take an LLC name from that register and search for Pennsylvania business entities, landing on the Department of State's free business search. The result exposes the filing date, active or inactive status, entity type, formation location, and address. Whitman then looks at the option to request the actual filings; the first company has only an initial filing. Their second example, Neshaminy Holding Corporation, is much less promising: a 1974 filing, an inactive dissolved status, and an address without further street information. Whitman explicitly says this may be a lead where nobody can be identified to speak with. Surplus Systems supplies the matching discipline for contact research: use full names, the property and previous addresses, county, state, and any available age or relative information. Their objective is not a large spreadsheet of numbers; it is the best way to reach the right person. Whitman's company example follows that practical distinction: a free entity record supplies additional information, but the dissolved-company result does not produce a confirmed human contact or a completed recovery. [0xk7lNvAgn0 @ 00:00:21] [0xk7lNvAgn0 @ 00:02:13] [RPpdYzSL6jE @ 00:01:17]

For deceased individuals, Overage Acquisition searches the owner's name plus obituary, checking funeral-home sites, legacy.com, and local newspaper archives. They take survivor names and cities into skiptracing.ai and TracerFi, claiming those platforms can return current mobile numbers and email addresses in under two minutes. Church adds a different first move: try the deceased person's listed mobile numbers because family members sometimes keep them. Their Lakeland search then extends to relatives, Facebook, LinkedIn, ancestry.com, legacy.com, and more specific obituary queries. Church also describes calling a care home or funeral provider and receiving callbacks from family members. The persistence becomes especially concrete in their separate elderly-owner case. Every number listed for the son failed, so Church individually skip-traced a relative and found the son's voicemail on that relative's last listed number. The son later explained that electronic documents were a problem, so Church switched to physical mail and discussed arranging a notary after review. Church describes most closing conversations as occurring between four and ten contacts, while that particular signing was still pending. The demonstrated sequence includes failed direct numbers, a second search through a relative, and a delivery method changed to match the claimant. [6vsHnTS609Y @ 00:01:16] [hA6VJ_GqGyc @ 00:00:39] [V_ycS3i_CMY @ 00:02:11]

Danielle's overseas recovery uses company information as a locating clue even though the land was owned in the individual's name. Mail had gone to an uncle's address and accumulated there. After nearly abandoning the search, Danielle switched from Google Chrome to DuckDuckGo, found information about the person and their company, and connected that information to Facebook. The resulting telephone number was a WhatsApp number. Danielle reports conducting the deal through messages and Google Translate without a telephone conversation. The claimant printed emailed documents and had them notarized, but the notarizations returned in Spanish; the county required English translations, so Danielle used a Spanish translating company. Church's deceased-owner outreach provides a parallel document mechanic: explain the required documents in a bullet-point list, arrange the notary, and give the family a clear next action. Where a claimant will not hand personal documents to Church, they describe letting the claimant send those documents directly to the county or state. Danielle's translation step and Church's direct-submission workaround both come from particular document obstacles, not from changing the claimant's identity or assuming that a successful conversation means the paperwork has already been accepted. [WEohyFOyk2M @ 00:00:39] [WEohyFOyk2M @ 00:02:19] [WEohyFOyk2M @ 00:03:15] [j97Qb2R6Efc @ 00:04:27]

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The clearest numerical conflict is inside Overage Acquisition's own affidavit playbook. In one presentation, the channel gives California's threshold as $28,850; in another, they state $166,250 during the explanation and later summarize California as $166,000. Both presentations list Nevada at $25,000 and Texas and Florida at $75,000. The channel's operational instruction is to find the threshold for the state being worked, and the $28,850 presentation explicitly says its figures were researched at recording time and may change. Overages Overflow emphasizes a different part of the release process: a death certificate alone often does not satisfy the holding office, which may require probate papers or a court order. Pierce Law Group describes proof of the personal representative's authority and a clerk's disbursement order in the North Carolina reverse-mortgage estate setting. These are different practitioner descriptions, not one agreed affidavit amount or one universal document package. Overage Acquisition sells the under-threshold route as the faster case selection strategy; Overages Overflow tells heirs to ask the holding office exactly what it needs; Pierce explains the representative's request and what happens when the proper payee is contested. [6vsHnTS609Y @ 00:04:47] [uw5ADHXVMX0 @ 00:04:50] [XTbc1Dz6dxY @ 00:01:32] [ErS3fgilrDY @ 00:00:48]

Appetite for labor-heavy estates also differs sharply. Overage Acquisition says they avoid probate cases unless the amount is substantial, naming $100,000 or more as their personal rule and describing a $5,000 overage with prolonged probate work as a poor use of time. Church, by contrast, investigates a difficult Lakeland file they correct to $14,000. For that unresolved case, they say they would request 50%, additional attorney fees, and offer their attorney about $1,500 plus 5% of what Church makes. Those are proposed terms, not a reported payment. Fullmer supplies a third approach: their $66,000 sibling case carried a 30% cut despite extensive family research, while their active $90,000 case required tracing beyond eight deceased children. Fullmer describes either contacting the remaining heirs and signing them or submitting a claim and sending notices to see whether they respond. They also offer partnership or referral as an alternative for operators lacking estate experience. The contrast is therefore case selection and division of work: Overage Acquisition filters toward larger probate amounts, Church contemplates a higher share for a smaller difficult file, and Fullmer treats family reconstruction and experienced collaboration as ways to pursue complicated estates. [6vsHnTS609Y @ 00:06:26] [hA6VJ_GqGyc @ 00:01:18] [zUGQVkbDEzc @ 00:01:35] [zUGQVkbDEzc @ 00:04:27]

Fees and persuasion are another genuine split. People Locator Skip Tracing says state database searches and claims are free, and locates professional value in identifying unknown deceased relatives or performing comprehensive cross-state searches. Church's Allstate-account call instead offers family assistance for 10% after payment, with nothing paid to Church if the recovery fails. Danielle initially asks the overseas owner for 30% and settles at 20% after the claimant describes bankruptcy and illness. Their negotiation includes saying a manager will not accept less than 20%; the interview then acknowledges that Danielle is that manager and the claimant does not know it. Church's separate outreach lesson takes a different line on factual claims: they describe a real two-week deadline on an older lead and explicitly say not to invent urgency because a prospect may check and lose trust. The accounts do not establish a single standard fee or a shared persuasion script. They show free self-service search, a contingent 10% insurance-account offer, and a negotiated 20% overseas recovery, alongside materially different ways of handling credibility, objections, and pressure during the conversation with the person who must sign. [mZfLBxhYGpw @ 00:01:48] [VGzK7EytsBw @ 00:01:46] [WEohyFOyk2M @ 00:04:43] [j97Qb2R6Efc @ 00:06:21]

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The locating failures are specific, not just a generic warning that some numbers will be wrong. Fullmer's difficult estate had no obituary, no children, and a married surname different from the siblings' names. They eventually found a niece, who revealed seven or eight surviving siblings. That experience cuts against Overage Acquisition's confidence that obituary searches nearly always produce the family road map. Church's elderly-owner case had a matching address but no usable direct number for the son; the breakthrough came only after individually searching a relative. Whitman's dissolved-company search ends with an equally concrete limitation: a historical filing and incomplete address without an identified person to contact. None of those files is solved merely by obtaining another search result. Fullmer reports a family connection that changed the case, Church reports a voicemail that finally reached the intended person, and Whitman leaves the company lead unresolved. Church's example then hits a second bottleneck after contact: documents sent electronically do not turn into signatures because the claimant is uncomfortable with computers. Mailing the papers addresses that obstacle, but Church still describes the signature and commission as future events rather than a finished payment. [zUGQVkbDEzc @ 00:00:50] [6vsHnTS609Y @ 00:01:16] [V_ycS3i_CMY @ 00:03:59] [0xk7lNvAgn0 @ 00:02:13]

Sean Bucci's active-claim death story shows how late a file can change. The couple had requested separate agreements for their respective halves. An HOA issue had already required paying some surplus to move the recovery forward, and the court then wanted a final document Bucci believes was a W-9. The mobile notary reached a hospital, where one claimant was dying. Bucci stopped the signing attempt rather than take time away from the couple's final moments together. The file already contained a will directing the property to the surviving spouse, but Bucci describes the post-foreclosure death as potentially requiring an estate or probate. Their attorney called the argument based on existing powers of attorney weak. Bucci later asked the surviving spouse how to issue the remaining check; the requested wording was the deceased claimant's name followed by estate. Whitman's explanation supplies the contrasting estate framing: the executor or administrator claims for the estate, not personally, and distribution follows estate liabilities. Bucci's reported resolution therefore remains a particular late-stage case involving existing documents, an attorney's assessment, and the surviving spouse's check instructions, rather than a universal instruction to continue using earlier powers of attorney after a claimant dies. [EPNAIRsvIHQ @ 00:00:39] [EPNAIRsvIHQ @ 00:02:34] [EPNAIRsvIHQ @ 00:04:04] [JRxMS-A2mXQ @ 00:01:50]

The economics checks start before anybody celebrates the headline amount. Danielle's overseas file falls from $97,000 to $87,000 after back taxes, then carries a negotiated 20% fee rather than the initial 30% request. That same claimant disappears for about a month while asking someone else to investigate, and the response they receive is that such recoveries do not happen in the United States. Danielle also incurs the additional translation task after Spanish notarizations reach the county. Church opens another presentation with a five-grand headline but immediately says the money has not technically been made; later they describe mailed documents, a hoped-for signature, and expected lawyer fees. Pierce Law Group explains an additional estate-stage constraint: the representative receives the funds, pays allowed estate expenses and valid claims in the required order, and only then distributes the remainder. Overages Overflow similarly warns that liens and estate debts can leave heirs little or nothing. The practitioners' reported checkpoints are therefore the amount after deductions, the actual signing status, unresolved document work, and the obligations ahead of heirs—not merely the surplus number that first attracted the operator to the file or the commission mentioned in a headline. [WEohyFOyk2M @ 00:01:14] [V_ycS3i_CMY @ 00:00:00] [ErS3fgilrDY @ 00:01:20] [XTbc1Dz6dxY @ 00:02:09]

chapters.question_prompt: How do I find usable contact information, organize outreach, and respond when people distrust the recovery offer?
chapters.title: Reach Claimants and Address Distrust
chapters.subtitle: Skip-tracing services, DNC screening, calling volume, lead follow-up, objection scripts, alternatives to calling, and pre-foreclosure Facebook ads.
chapters.executive_summary: The practitioners converge on better contact data, repeated contact, concrete evidence, and a clear explanation of contingency fees. Eric Richardson describes 150–200 daily leads with dialing software, while David Church farms smaller groups and follows unfinished claims. Shawn Bougie uses deeds, tax mailing addresses, relatives, and returned envelopes to find displaced owners. David Wilkerson favors bulk data preparation and repeated offers; Richardson instead makes proof the first-call priority. Their disagreements matter: Spencer Vann accepts free searches for cash-constrained beginners, Bougie rejects cheap data, and Joe Green's mutual-friend tactic is precisely the approach Bougie criticizes. Richardson's DNC lawsuit changes the outreach discussion. Caleb Luketic supplies a separate inbound play: $25–$40 pre-foreclosure leads generated through a helpful guide rather than a cash-offer pitch.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: A claimant's first question is often why a stranger found money that the claimant never heard about. Israel Miller opens by acknowledging the exact reaction to an unexpected text about a property the recipient no longer owns. Miller explains surplus as the difference between the debt behind an auction and the higher sale price, then explains why notices can miss former owners: the letter goes to the foreclosed residence, or its legal language gets set aside. Miller's offer is research, paperwork, and the claim process on contingency, with nothing charged upfront and a percentage collected only after recovery. Nick Fullmer describes the same basic business: monitor sales, identify an overage, find the former homeowner, and help reunite that person with the funds. Fullmer also points to notices sent to the lost property as a reason owners remain unaware. Richardson's answer to distrust is not a faster pitch. The first call establishes identity, confirms the correct person, and asks for an email address so the claimant can inspect the details independently. The common operating position is specific: explain where the money came from, explain why the message is unexpected, and show what the recovery service actually does before asking the person to trust it. Surplus_Prosperity [MYo3k2Sxj1Q @ 00:01:54]; Nick Fullmer- Overage Syndicate [QDRGMRtpIOs @ 00:04:18]; Money Making Juggernaut [rJjMD-YvK30 @ 00:01:37].

Finding a usable number starts with finding the right person, not merely buying a search result. Shawn Bougie describes former owners living in cars, with parents, or on a friend's couch; those moves make current credit-header contact information harder to obtain. Bougie favors IDI Data for claimant phone numbers, addresses, and emails, and Microbilt for possible relatives and associates. David Wilkerson likewise treats accurate data as an operating investment rather than a place to save pennies regardless of results. Wilkerson prepares data in bulk because repeatedly chasing tiny lists, stripping spreadsheet columns, and building a master key interrupts prospecting. Sunday afternoon or another low-contact period is the time Wilkerson assigns to that work. Spencer Vann also connects better data with fewer wasted calls, while framing the purchase around available time and capital. Vann reports hearing of one correct number in fifty or one hundred calls with True People Search, versus one in five, seven, or ten with services such as TLO or IDI Core. Those are Vann's reported experiences from conversations, not a single shared test across the services. Across these approaches, usable contact information includes more than the first phone number: Bougie explicitly values addresses, email, and relatives when the direct route does not reach the claimant. SurplusFundsRiches [ujbTh1In_c4 @ 00:00:41]; Surplus Funds 101 [xqXetexqH30 @ 00:00:57]; Spencer Vann [ZTs6XQ9lr-c @ 00:02:22].

Repeated contact is central to both small-list farming and higher-volume calling. David Church starts with ten leads from a list and works them rather than treating the entire list as a single pass. Church reports success in late morning and early afternoon, while saying many successful people Church coaches reach prospects between eight and nine or after five. A morning attempt followed by an evening callback is a specific pattern Church favors. Richardson similarly describes calls, voicemail, texts, and later double-tap follow-up instead of blasting through numbers once. Church keeps unreached names on paper or a Google sheet, recording attempted numbers, and reserves the CRM for people actually contacted. That differs from Richardson's imported-lead dialing workflow, but both keep contact attempts connected to subsequent action. Wilkerson adds that a conversation needs an offer: summarize what was discussed and ask whether paperwork can be sent and whether a notary visit tomorrow or Friday works better. Wilkerson emphasizes contact rate and offer rate over clever one-liners. The overlap is sustained work, not a universal script or identical database setup. Church's pipeline includes old conversations alongside new claims; Richardson's workflow combines channels; Wilkerson's closing habit prevents an otherwise useful conversation from ending without an explicit next step. Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds [gApaLMe_Eec @ 00:03:58]; Money Making Juggernaut [JQrEcneXSbk @ 00:03:24]; Surplus Funds 101 [-A2pNSevACs @ 00:04:35].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Bougie's search sequence starts wide: first and last name plus the property address, initially leaving out the middle name and directional components such as northwest or southeast. If the match fails, tighten the search or change the address. The deed may show a mailing address different from the property, particularly when the purchase was an investment or for someone else. The tax assessor's card is another source of a separate notification address. Bougie repeatedly asks for these records because they provide additional reference points for finding the correct owner. Bougie also checks returned mail for 'forwarding order expired'; the return can include the destination address that had previously been used. For live contact through another person, White Pages Premium is Bougie's reverse-address option: a renter still at the property may supply the former owner's contact details. Wilkerson's bulk alternative is Batch Lead Stacker, quoted at about forty dollars monthly and fifteen cents per skip trace. Wilkerson says it does not charge for no-hit files or duplicate leads and remembers identifying details across uploads. The workflows differ in scale, but the actions are concrete: prepare the identifying records, search against more than one address when needed, and retain useful information from failed delivery rather than treating every returned envelope as the end of the search. SurplusFundsRiches [bt6FqwHwtBY @ 00:00:30]; SurplusFundsRiches [ujbTh1In_c4 @ 00:03:29]; Surplus Funds 101 [xqXetexqH30 @ 00:03:05].

Richardson budgets two to three hours for a solo operator, describing two hours of calls and one hour of research. Manual dialing produces about fifty calls in the stated daily routine; the software-assisted target is 150–200 leads. Richardson names Batch Dialer and PhoneBurner as alternatives charging roughly one hundred to one hundred thirty dollars monthly per seat, then describes Excess Elite's built-in dialer without an additional seat charge. Leads must be imported in the correct format. The workflow leaves a voicemail when possible and sends a text suited to the recipient: a former owner receives a property-related message, while a relative receives a relationship-confirmation message. Richardson separately reports changing outreach after a DNC lawsuit, filtering DNC-listed contacts, not using voicemail drops or auto dialers, and using a one-number-at-a-time power dialer. These are different descriptions from Richardson, not interchangeable instructions about the same dialing behavior. Church's smaller-list version records attempts before CRM entry, makes callbacks at different times, and uses specific email subjects such as the property address and account information. Church starts involving relatives after two or three unsuccessful attempts, describing a check associated with the property rather than announcing an embarrassing foreclosure to family members. Both practitioners describe follow-up as part of the work, not something left to memory after an unanswered call. Money Making Juggernaut [JQrEcneXSbk @ 00:01:17]; Money Making Juggernaut [Zh5fus4SGzc @ 00:02:21]; Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds [gApaLMe_Eec @ 00:05:30].

Richardson's proof package contains county sale results, the state-law reference, the court record, and the business website. The first-call response is straightforward: the claimant need not take a stranger's word for it, nothing is charged upfront, and the records can be reviewed independently. Richardson also says not to ask for Social Security or bank information on that call. For the objection that all the money went to debt, Richardson demonstrates the arithmetic with fifteen thousand dollars in taxes and a fifty-thousand-dollar sale, leaving thirty-five thousand before other possible debts; Richardson says to check liens before calling. For fear of theft, explain the actual payment path through the county, court, or trustee and, in many cases, an attorney escrow account distributing according to the signed agreement. Miller's text-to-video approach also explains the contingency arrangement and then asks for a short form covering state, sale type, and approximate timing. Church opens with the specific account, address, and check rather than small talk, then explains ongoing case follow-up and document handling as the service. Church asks permission to email agreements and arrange a notary. Each practitioner gives the claimant something concrete to evaluate: records, a recognizable account, a stated payment arrangement, or an identifiable next action. Money Making Juggernaut [rJjMD-YvK30 @ 00:02:22]; Surplus_Prosperity [MYo3k2Sxj1Q @ 00:04:08]; Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds [jNXoU7Ep1vY @ 00:03:46].

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The data-buying disagreement is explicit. Bougie says to get a real service and quotes one dollar fifty to six dollars per search even in bulk, depending on depth. Free services and penny searches are precisely what Bougie rejects. Vann does not require every beginner to start at the expensive end. Vann puts True People Search, Fast People Search, and basic White Pages at one end, with TLO and IDI Core toward the other, and asks whether time or money is the limiting resource. A person with more time and less money may start with free searches or lower-priced services such as BeenVerified; someone with less time and more capital may move up. Vann also says access requirements can take weeks and recommends speaking with the provider before creating a business entity, so the required documents are understood. Wilkerson's choice is different again: bulk Batch Lead Stacker data, with no-hit and duplicate exclusions central to the economics. These practitioners are not quoting one universal market price or naming one unanimous winner. Bougie emphasizes deeper claimant research, Vann emphasizes entry-point tradeoffs and onboarding friction, and Wilkerson emphasizes recurring batch preparation and the charges avoided when lists overlap or a search produces no telephone number. SurplusFundsRiches [bt6FqwHwtBY @ 00:00:13]; Spencer Vann [ZTs6XQ9lr-c @ 00:03:51]; Surplus Funds 101 [xqXetexqH30 @ 00:03:24].

Objection handling divides between immediate proof, staged resistance handling, and aggressive persistence. Richardson says pressure fails when someone calls the offer a scam; send evidence and give the claimant room to verify it. Wilkerson calls many objections buyer questions in disguise, but treats the first complaint as something to ignore while continuing the presentation. On its second appearance, Wilkerson acknowledges it, answers briefly, then drops and diverts. The third appearance becomes a true objection: repeat it, explain in detail, ask for remaining questions, and tie down the answer before moving on. Church educates first, presents the service, and follows people who say they will claim independently. Church describes asking to check back in three or four weeks, then says the callback still happens even if the person says not to. Richardson draws the opposite line on an explicit stop: stop and put the person on the do-not-call list that day. This is a direct disagreement, not merely a different tone. Church also distinguishes ordinary moved-account owners from people discovering inherited accounts, saying the latter more often use the service. Richardson accepts that people can file themselves in simple cases and argues for the service through paperwork, deadlines, and difficult claims rather than denying that option. Money Making Juggernaut [rJjMD-YvK30 @ 00:13:18]; Surplus Funds 101 [z_Y10SDCdp4 @ 00:03:35]; Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds [jNXoU7Ep1vY @ 00:03:59].

Joe Green's alternatives are letters, emails, social media, holiday cards, and local visits. Green handwrites envelopes, uses email subjects that feel conversational, and describes Snow Greeting Cards for personalized-looking cards mailed by the service. Green's Facebook tactic is to connect with a lead's friends and relatives first, so the eventual request appears to come from someone already connected to familiar people. Bougie specifically objects to that friend-of-a-friend method, calling it a business relationship started through deceit. Green's local play is a brief doorstep delivery within about twenty miles: confirm the name, hand over a black envelope, introduce the service, and leave contact details rather than occupying much time. Green favors this more for state funds than tax overages. Caleb Luketic offers a separate pre-foreclosure seller-acquisition workflow: Facebook selfie-style ads offer a state-specific guide of about seventeen pages instead of a cash offer. The form asks whether the homeowner wants to sell and how far behind payments are. Leads enter seller, information-gathering, or MLS-listed tracks. GoHighLevel handles guide delivery and follow-up, with interested sellers handed to acquisitions. Luketic describes follow-up lasting over two years for undecided leads and stopping at close; the reported twenty-five-to-forty-dollar cost belongs to that pre-foreclosure campaign. Unclaimed CEO [WlbnzGtdoSY @ 00:02:21]; SurplusFundsRiches [bt6FqwHwtBY @ 00:03:29]; Caleb Luketic [oGjbQZW0yuA @ 00:04:27].

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Richardson's DNC account is a reversal grounded in a lawsuit, not a theoretical warning. Richardson says calls went unscrubbed from the start of the business in 2018 until about September 2024 because the requirement was not understood, and says most skip-tracing providers were not performing a DNC check. The contact concerned an entity owed surplus and its registered agent, whose phone number was publicly available. Richardson believed the business-to-business context supported the contact, yet the other party filed a federal case and brought a class action. Richardson stresses the cost of defending the case regardless of who was right. The forty-thousand-dollar figure is the attorney's described potential cost of fighting through court and depositions, not a reported settlement payment. Richardson reports paying three thousand dollars for specialist training, then describes DNC filtering, no voicemail drops, and one-at-a-time power dialing. Luketic also reports being sued over an offer-check letter sent through ordinary direct mail, before explaining the move toward inbound pre-foreclosure leads. Bougie adds a separate data-handling burden: providers may require annual testing, a verifiable business location, and secure handling of regulated information. Bougie describes destroying regulated material with a cross-cut shredder or a destruction company when disposing of the file, rather than simply discarding it intact. Money Making Juggernaut [Zh5fus4SGzc @ 00:00:29]; Caleb Luketic [oGjbQZW0yuA @ 00:00:25]; SurplusFundsRiches [L0EsEWU9jis @ 00:06:40].

A friendly conversation is not the same as returned paperwork. Church describes an older claimant who sounded enthusiastic, requested documents, and then claimed directly. Church had prepared everything before checking the state record and discovering the claim was already made. The experience sits beside Church's stronger follow-up results: a two-hundred-sixty-thousand-dollar stock claim involved at least six or seven conversations, and two previously contacted clients returned paperwork during a week when Church made no new-deal calls. Church's point is that an old pipeline can produce work, while some apparently agreeable prospects still go around the service. Wilkerson supplies a separate comparison from two virtual assistants given the same number of leads. One averaged two weekly deals with no cancellations; the other averaged six or seven with two cancellations. Wilkerson describes the latter as ending with four transactions rather than two and emphasizes the net number remaining. Wilkerson also says excessive cancellations can signal pushiness, while none may mean the list is not being fully worked. Richardson's reported Ashley example adds another timescale: a skeptical claimant required six months of friendly follow-up on a one-hundred-ninety-six-thousand-dollar surplus, producing about fifty-eight-thousand-eight-hundred dollars at a thirty percent fee. The practitioners describe both patient wins and work that never becomes a paid recovery. Surplus Institute / David Church / Unclaimed Funds [jNXoU7Ep1vY @ 00:07:36]; Surplus Funds 101 [-A2pNSevACs @ 00:08:26]; Money Making Juggernaut [rJjMD-YvK30 @ 00:02:50].

Access and search quality can consume the time an operator expected to spend talking with claimants. Vann describes TLO's company verification, office or home inspection, and paper-shredder checks as burdensome despite valuing the data. Vann says the onboarding process can take weeks and warns that Fiverr or Upwork sellers may advertise TLO access while actually using True People Search. Vann describes outsourced searching as hit-or-miss, not a dependable shortcut simply because a seller names a premium database. Bougie reports another bottleneck: overseas researchers may lack the U.S. address, company setup, and banking arrangements needed to obtain the services directly, which is why some research for Bougie's operation instead. Even a good database can miss an owner when courthouse information is not refreshed frequently or the owner did not live at the property. Bougie therefore returns to the original deed and separate notification address rather than assuming the first no-hit settles the matter. Wilkerson's financial check is equally specific: recurring duplicate leads and searches without hits affect what the data actually costs, which is why those exclusions matter in the chosen subscription. Wilkerson reports having spent more than thirty thousand dollars on skip tracing and emphasizes consistent usable data, batch preparation, and avoiding repeated charges rather than evaluating a platform only by its monthly membership price. Spencer Vann [ZTs6XQ9lr-c @ 00:04:38]; Spencer Vann [ZTs6XQ9lr-c @ 00:07:53]; SurplusFundsRiches [L0EsEWU9jis @ 00:07:07]; Surplus Funds 101 [xqXetexqH30 @ 00:04:02].

chapters.question_prompt: What should I say on a surplus-funds call, and what can I learn from practitioners' live conversations and call critiques?
chapters.title: The Surplus-Funds Call: Scripts and Live Examples
chapters.subtitle: First-call objectives, credible introductions, conversation structure, common calling mistakes, callbacks, and recorded closing examples.
chapters.executive_summary: Eric Richardson, Alfred Taren, David Church, and Bob Diamond put credible information, patient listening, and a concrete next step ahead of a hard opening pitch. Richardson targets an initial call under five minutes; Taren opens with auction results and pauses; Church leads with identifying data. Their follow-up expectations differ: Richardson describes three to ten follow-ups after documents, while Diamond describes two or three conversations plus other communications. The sharper disagreements concern detailed versus curiosity-driven voicemail, immediate closing versus sending proof first, and how much pressure to apply after rejection. Live examples also separate agreement to receive paperwork from completed recovery: Church calls a $16,000 day verbal commissions with contracts still unsigned, and Spencer Vann describes a first-call result as a potential deal.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The opening job is to explain why this particular person is hearing from you, not to perform a generic sales introduction. Eric Richardson of Money Making Juggernaut reduces the first call to four pillars: introduce yourself, verify the former owner, explain what happened and how the company helps, then collect an email or mailing address. The point is to deliver proof rather than stretch a stranger's attention into a long presentation [JJObKyLY5YY @ 00:00:59]. Surplus Funds Secrets describes the same underlying trust problem from the recipient's side: why are you calling, how did you get the number, why would money exist, and does this mean another debt? Their preferred opening identifies funds that may be owed to the person or their family's estate before asking whether it is a good time to talk [HtbOqZK2He8 @ 00:00:30]. Bob Diamond adds that skepticism is expected, not an objection that disappears because the amount sounds attractive. Diamond asks callers to let people move at their own pace and explains the eventual request as written permission and a short notary meeting, with payment dependent on successful recovery. The shared approach is information first, room for questions, and a manageable next action—not an instant demand for trust [NOkg0U0k9Zs @ 00:00:11].

Credibility begins with identifying details the recipient can recognize. Alfred Taren wants the sale date, sale price, and approximate amount owed ready before dialing. Taren's opening concerns the auction results for the property, followed by a request to go over those numbers. The caller then pauses instead of burying the person under explanation [CqlbwGPmv64 @ 00:00:34]. David Church similarly describes a direct introduction built around the person's name, an account, and an address. Church's example is an unclaimed CD account, not a foreclosure surplus; the attention-getting mechanism is the recognizable data, followed by what the service can do for that person. Church explicitly rejects leading with a personal résumé or family story because the recipient wants to know why the call matters to them [alaKJIcbbLw @ 00:00:42]. Richardson's property verification serves another purpose: two people can share a name, so the caller must establish that the person actually owned the relevant property. Richardson follows verification with engaging questions about whether the person knew about the funds or had already been contacted. Those questions make the call a conversation and keep the information in a deliberate order. A familiar name alone is not Richardson's verification, and a confident voice alone is not Taren's evidence [JJObKyLY5YY @ 00:01:28].

Agreement also extends beyond the first conversation: paperwork and callbacks need active attention. David Wilkerson of Surplus Funds 101 says most accounts arrive at contact points three through five, not the initial contact. Wilkerson asks for an email, offers screenshots of the account documentation, and usually aims for a Zoom conversation as the second contact because seeing the other person adds credibility. When someone is already ready for the notary, however, Wilkerson says to close rather than force another appointment [smhFDkvMwkM @ 00:03:54]. Richardson's review of Morgan's call gives a different follow-up measure: after sending documents, expect three to ten follow-ups before signed papers return, while recognizing immediate returns as exceptions. Richardson praises collecting both the email and current mailing address, not merely getting a friendly response [MbdEoM3KDC0 @ 00:04:15]. Diamond describes two or three actual conversations combined with letters, texts, and emails, totaling roughly six or seven communications before signup. Diamond's examples include a reminder before an agreed callback. These are different descriptions of contact activity, not interchangeable counts of cold calls. What they share is a next step that remains visible after the phone disconnects: deliver the material, keep the appointment, and continue the conversation until the person actually acts [NOkg0U0k9Zs @ 00:01:18].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Richardson's working script starts simply: 'Hello, is this John?' Then comes the caller's name and company, the property address, and the question of previous ownership. Richardson anchors the sale event before asking whether anyone has contacted the person about surplus funds, excess proceeds, overages, or remaining funds. The destination is explicit: 'What I'd like to do is send you the details so that you can see this for yourself. What's the best email for you?' Richardson says the first call is for sending proof, not forcing a close [DMdtmrWAO6c @ 00:06:34]. Taren offers a quieter alternative opening: 'I'm reading about the auction results for the property on Main Street.' After asking permission to review the figures, Taren waits three to five seconds if necessary, then describes the difference between the sale and opening bid as possible funds rather than definite proceeds [CqlbwGPmv64 @ 00:01:26]. Surplus Funds Secrets supplies the transition from explanation to paperwork: describe engagement documents as the step that lets the team begin working on the recovery, then offer a digital or in-person notary at the client's convenience. Their closing question is whether today or tomorrow works best. Each script gives the recipient something specific to answer instead of requiring them to absorb an uninterrupted monologue [i7mng3-o1u0 @ 00:02:39].

Before that conversation, Richardson sorts the phone numbers rather than assuming the first skip-traced result is correct. Call each listed number to identify disconnected lines, cross those out, then text the live numbers with a first-name question such as 'Hello, is this John?' Wrong-number replies remove more candidates. Richardson then runs a call, voicemail, and text sequence, repeating the process and extending it to relatives [DMdtmrWAO6c @ 00:03:05]. After an email goes out, Richardson texts that it has been sent and calls within ten minutes to walk through it [DMdtmrWAO6c @ 00:09:03]. Church's desk preparation is more basic but equally concrete: rehearse the script twenty times and keep the Google Voice number visible because Church sometimes starts giving a personal cell number instead. The visible reference also supports answering unexpected questions without losing the thread [alaKJIcbbLw @ 00:03:03]. Spencer Vann keeps the script in front of them even though they wrote it. In the live calling session, Vann also recommends printed leads for crossing people out and noting voicemail or conversation outcomes. The reason is practical recall while moving through the list, not a claim that printed paper replaces every other tracking method. Both callers describe references they actually use while speaking [JjEdRqLg0Ug @ 00:04:45].

The live fee conversations attach the percentage to a service and a next step. Dexter Brown describes a possible recovery around $15,000, then explains a thirty-percent company share and seventy-percent client share. Brown divides the company's share into ten points each for research, locating, and legal work, and says payment occurs only if money is recovered [0FZrtOY2H5w @ 00:04:49]. Brown then offers paperwork delivery or email, a conversation with another family member, and a shared email thread and DocuSign so the participants receive the material together [0FZrtOY2H5w @ 00:07:56]. In Morgan's call reviewed by Richardson, the caller describes about $29,000 available and quotes a normal percentage of twenty-five to thirty, depending on the arrangement. Morgan asks for current contact details and offers overnight documents with return postage, keeping the immediate task on reviewing and returning the packet [MbdEoM3KDC0 @ 00:01:34]. Church's commission-day examples use a different arrangement: ten percent paid to JD Vista from the recovery, with the state paying the claimant directly. Church offers to email forms and start paperwork, including a power-of-attorney situation. These are the speakers' particular fee conversations, not one universal surplus-funds price. The repeated operational move is explaining the arrangement before asking the person to proceed [ieI6zKICpKo @ 00:00:59].

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Voicemail is a direct disagreement. Richardson wants a short message containing the caller's name, company, and property address, with no money talk. Richardson argues that curiosity produces callbacks while too much detail can trigger suspicion and blocking [DMdtmrWAO6c @ 00:03:51]. Vann uses the same withholding approach: an important piece of information about the old property, not an announcement that money is owed. Vann explicitly calls the voicemail a hook [JjEdRqLg0Ug @ 00:03:40]. Church goes the other way in the state-unclaimed-funds session, describing detailed messages that identify the account, address, company, and reason for contact. Church attributes much of the business to those callbacks and describes the returning caller as a warm lead [xqpLsq3JVlU @ 00:50:30]. Yet Church uses less information when facing a screening prompt: say the recipient's name followed by 'it's' and stop, letting curiosity encourage pickup. Church says this recently adopted technique works well and gives a nine-out-of-ten pickup claim during the explanation. That screening tactic is distinct from Church's detailed voicemail practice, and the examples come from a session devoted to state unclaimed funds. The callers do not offer a single shared rule about how much information belongs in every unanswered-call situation [xqpLsq3JVlU @ 00:23:43].

Pace and emotional preparation also vary. Richardson's first-call target is five minutes or less, with the narrow goal of putting proof in the recipient's hands [JJObKyLY5YY @ 00:00:27]. Church describes the 'perfect' conversation as sixteen minutes and credits listening for receiving mailing details, an email, and extensive family information. The conversation then expands into additional unclaimed accounts rather than stopping at the original returned insurance check [MsxVzoHQCNk @ 00:08:08]. Vann emphasizes certainty, directness, and questions that connect a recovery to the person's financial circumstances. Vann's example asks what an extra $20,000 would mean after a pandemic-related income loss, before presenting the service. This is emotional discovery about the recovery, not weather or sports small talk [ZEobF_ck678 @ 00:11:42]. Wilkerson is more explicit about rapport and urgency: move quickly through people who are not deals, then slow down when a collectible account, receptiveness, and need come together. Wilkerson also says not to push a willing signer into a second appointment merely because the usual process includes one. The contrast is therefore not simply short calls against long calls. Richardson defines a proof-first objective; Church follows useful disclosures; Vann develops the personal meaning of recovery; Wilkerson adjusts pace to readiness [smhFDkvMwkM @ 00:04:15].

Family cases expose a sharper difference between conversational shortcuts and questions about authority. Brown's Louisiana call concerns a deceased owner with several children and a large extended family. Brown presents a small succession as cheaper than a regular succession and describes two heirs stating that they are the only heirs they know of. Brown also expressly says the approach should not be used maliciously to cut people out; the cost argument and that warning both belong to Brown's pitch [0FZrtOY2H5w @ 00:02:30]. Taren takes a different line when speaking with relatives: establish whether the person is a spouse, child, or executor, ask whether probate has started, and do not decide on the phone how the family splits the funds. Taren distinguishes being family from having the right to claim [CqlbwGPmv64 @ 00:05:18]. Church describes having encountered relatives who wanted payment even though a spouse had never divorced the deceased person. That experience leads Church to ask about marriage, children, wills, and documentation before making promises about the recipient. In the returned-insurance-check conversation, Church also asks about power of attorney and supporting paperwork. These accounts offer materially different family conversations, with Church and Taren emphasizing questions that Brown's abbreviated succession explanation moves through quickly [MsxVzoHQCNk @ 00:04:16].

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Wrong connections and calling friction appear throughout Church's long live session. Church notices California leads would receive a six-in-the-morning Saturday call and moves away from that timing. Later, Google Voice does not connect as expected, prompting attempts from other lines. A supposed family connection also proves wrong: the person does not recognize the deceased account holder, and Church eventually accepts that the association is bad rather than treating the denial as a successful identification [xqpLsq3JVlU @ 00:57:28]. Taren's preparation addresses the timing side directly: use the recipient's time zone, call between eight in the morning and about nine at night, and consider an earlier evening cutoff for elderly recipients. Taren also says to note a request not to call again and stop calling [CqlbwGPmv64 @ 00:00:51]. Richardson finds a different missed-contact trap in Morgan's call: the phone rings about eight times before the person answers. Richardson says ending after four rings would have lost that conversation. The three examples are not the same failure. One is a false association, another is bad timing, and another is abandoning a ringing line too soon. Each comes from an identified event or explicit calling instruction, rather than a blanket claim that every unanswered number is worthless [MbdEoM3KDC0 @ 00:04:57].

Trust can fail after the recipient has already agreed to listen. In Church's skeptical-family conversation, the person describes frightening reports about another recovery company and worries about bank information. Church responds with public records, company and attorney credentials, paperwork, and checks mailed without requesting routing or banking information. Church also admits cutting off a discussion of a sudden death and says more empathy was needed [87zmv7-0D7s @ 00:10:17]. Fee language creates another problem in Church's returned-insurance-check review: saying the state pays the company could sound as though the ten percent is additional money. Church corrects the explanation to say the fee comes from the recovered funds, and reports that another prospect had recently decided to claim independently [MsxVzoHQCNk @ 00:07:30]. Wilkerson warns against trying to establish credibility through phrases such as '100% legit' or 'scam free,' saying they can produce the opposite reaction. Wilkerson also writes notes during calls and transfers them to the CRM afterward, keeping follow-up grounded in the actual conversation. The practical reversals are specific: talking over grief, making payment sound different from its actual source, and using defensive labels that make the caller seem less credible. Church's own example also shows that explaining the opportunity does not prevent a person from proceeding without the locator [smhFDkvMwkM @ 00:08:17].

A promising call and collected commission are different events in the practitioners' own accounts. Church announces $16,000 from four $40,000 opportunities, but immediately identifies the amount as verbal commissions and says contracts still need signing. One opportunity came from a callback, another from follow-up, and two from first-time conversations [ieI6zKICpKo @ 00:00:00]. Vann's live first-call success likewise ends with permission to email information and investigate whether money remains after an earlier collection. At the end, Vann calls the result a potential deal rather than reporting a recovered check [JjEdRqLg0Ug @ 00:05:17]. Church is equally explicit in the skeptical-family review: the person moves from resisting contact to requesting the information, but Church says the deal is still being worked and the outcome is not known [87zmv7-0D7s @ 00:12:27]. Rejection also carries a production cost. Vann recalls an early probate-property cold call ending in an extended angry response; Vann stopped calling for the rest of that day. The later lesson was to celebrate getting through rejection and continue toward people willing to engage. That story concerns Vann's earlier real-estate calling, while the lesson is applied to surplus-funds conversations: do not let one hostile exchange end the work [ZEobF_ck678 @ 00:06:27].

chapters.question_prompt: What agreements, claim forms, signatures, and post-signing steps are needed to move a recovery toward filing?
chapters.title: From Signed Agreement to Claim Submission
chapters.subtitle: Contract walkthroughs, document checklists, Florida tax-deed forms, affidavits, mobile notaries, attorney-free filing discussions, and post-signing handoffs.
chapters.executive_summary: The practitioners agree on the foundation: a signed fee agreement starts the case, but the money holder's requirements determine the filing packet. Eric Richardson, Alfred Taren, and Nick Fullmer reject universal paperwork; Greg at Overage Acquisition shows the deed purchase and tracked mailing that follow a returned contract. David Church walks clients through agreements rather than leaving signatures to chance. Reported costs include roughly $4 for Greg's deed copy, $25 for Fullmer's remote notarization, and Bob Diamond's $1,800–$2,000 judicial-claim budget. Their approaches diverge on attorney involvement, certified deeds, mobile versus remote notarization, and whether to submit early or assemble every required original first. Missing death certificates, incorrect ink, competing interests, and silent follow-up turn signed business into stalled business.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: A signed agreement starts the recovery; it does not finish the claim. Coach Brown at Surplus Systems makes that distinction operational: check every required field, signature, and date, confirm the claimant and case information, and keep a clear copy before moving forward. The next job is to turn that agreement into an organized case containing property details, claimant contact information, supporting documents, required forms, and a checklist of unfinished work [TA1G1Ejrb0M @ 00:01:15]. Nick Fullmer puts the fee agreement at the foundation because it establishes the operator's compensation and what the client receives; everything beyond that depends on the location and whether the money came from a tax sale or mortgage foreclosure [-KBy24CSPOw @ 00:01:54]. David Church attacks the same handoff from the client side. Rather than emailing an agreement and hoping it returns, Church asks whether the client is at a computer and has time to read it together. They explain the next signatures and supporting documents while the client is actually looking at the agreement [A47AbsTHlkY @ 00:02:46]. These approaches share a concrete starting point: the compensation arrangement must be understood, the signed document must be usable, and the next action must be explicit. Brown's checklist and Church's walkthrough both keep a verbal yes from becoming an unattended piece of paperwork.

The strongest agreement is that the receiving office determines the packet. Eric Richardson rejects a cookie-cutter checklist because tax sales, mortgage foreclosures, deceased owners, multiple owners, companies, and trusts produce different requirements. Their first move is to find the county's instructions, ask what it requires, and establish whether it accepts originals, email, or another submission method [JLCbKq99rGE @ 00:01:24]. Alfred Taren separates two questions that operators often collapse: who physically holds the money, and whether release requires an administrative form or a court petition. The first identifies the destination; the second identifies the procedure. Taren insists on answering both for the specific sale type and state [ouYE5P3UJdQ @ 00:03:35]. Overage Acquisition's Greg reaches the same practical conclusion through their California work: counties may request similar documents without accepting identical ones. Their Los Angeles example requires the county's own assignment form rather than Greg's usual version [XWtB0RDJ1wE @ 00:02:33]. That distinction matters even after a client has signed your agreement. The client relationship and the county's release requirements are different parts of the job. Richardson starts with instructions, Taren starts with the holder and procedure, and Greg keeps county-specific forms together. None describes a generic agreement as a substitute for the receiving office's actual filing requirements or supporting-document checklist.

The shared document logic is identity, interest, authority, and a correctly completed claim. Noble Notary & Legal Document Preparers walks through Florida tax-deed fields that connect a person to a particular sale: contact details, tax deed number, parcel number, sale date, claimant status, and the recorded instrument supporting the interest. Their supporting-document discussion adds identification, the deed or lien instrument, a W-9, and notarized authorization when someone files for another person [DM0kjEZlbSk @ 00:04:44]. Bob Diamond describes the administrative version as an agency form carrying property and claimant information, accompanied by identification, then reviewed by the office holding the money [6ElvJMKfF9g @ 00:00:27]. The claimtaxsaleoverages guide defines the claimant as the person or entity eligible to claim, typically the former owner, and emphasizes that the filing deadline can determine whether recovery remains available [e309errLsBw @ 00:02:10]. Their common ground is not that every office asks for an identical stack. It is that the packet must identify the eligible claimant, connect that claimant to the property and sale, and reach the right office within its filing window. Noble's detailed fields supply the mechanics; Diamond's account supplies the administrative sequence. A signed commercial agreement belongs beside that evidence, not in place of the recorded ownership documents or the office's claim form.
